title: Your Cosmic Address
objective: After this level you can state Earth's address: third planet from the Sun, a star in the Milky Way.
summary: The Sun is a star, Earth is planet three, and our whole solar system lives in the Milky Way.

cards.headline: Every star you see at night is a sun. Ours is just the closest one.
cards.body: That little twinkle you wish on? It's a sun. It looks tiny for one reason only: it's unbelievably far away.

cards.headline: Your cosmic mailing address
cards.body: If aliens wanted to mail you a postcard, they'd need a long address. Line one: Earth. Line two: the third planet from the Sun, with two neighbors closer in and five farther out. Line three: the solar system, which is just the Sun plus everything swinging around it. And we're not done yet.

mascot.line: You're always seeing the Sun a little late. I've been late my whole life, so this one I love.

cards.fact: The Sun you see is 8 minutes old.
cards.context: Sunlight takes about 8 minutes to reach us, so the Sun in the sky is the Sun from 8 minutes ago. If it vanished right now, you'd keep seeing it for about 8 more minutes. Light is the fastest thing there is. The Sun is just that far away.

cards.headline: Last line: the Milky Way
cards.body: The final line on the envelope is the Milky Way, a spiral of at least 100 billion stars. We live out in the suburbs, about 26,000 light-years from downtown. On a dark night, that hazy stripe across the sky is the rest of our galaxy. You're looking at your own neighborhood from the sidewalk.

title: The Sun, Up Close
objective: After this level you can explain what powers the Sun and how dominant it is in the solar system.
summary: The Sun fuses hydrogen into helium, holds 99.8% of the solar system's mass, and is about 4.6 billion years old.

cards.headline: The Sun isn't on fire. It's doing something far stranger.
cards.body: Picture the Sun as a giant bonfire? Wrong picture. It has been shining for about 4.6 billion years, and no fire lasts that long. Something much stranger is going on inside.

cards.headline: A star that squeezes atoms
cards.body: Deep in the Sun's core it's about 15 million °C. At that heat, hydrogen atoms slam together so hard that they fuse into helium, and every crash releases a tiny spark of energy. One spark is nothing. But the core does this an almost unimaginable number of times every second, and all those sparks add up to every bit of sunshine you've ever felt.

cards.fact: The Sun holds about 99.8% of the solar system's mass.
cards.context: Every planet, moon, asteroid and comet put together? That's the other 0.2%. We're the crumbs. If the Sun were as tall as your front door, Earth would be about the size of a nickel. No wonder everything circles it: the Sun's gravity is what holds the whole solar system together.

cards.headline: Middle-aged, not old
cards.body: 4.6 billion years sounds ancient, until you learn that a star like ours can keep fusing hydrogen for about 10 billion years. So the Sun isn't old at all. It's middle-aged, with billions of good years of shining still ahead of it.

title: The Rocky Four
objective: After this level you can name the rocky planets and explain why Venus, not Mercury, is the hottest.
summary: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are rocky. Venus is the hottest planet thanks to its heat-trapping atmosphere, and Mars is red because of rust.

cards.headline: Mercury is closest to the Sun. So why is Venus hotter?
cards.body: You'd bet on Mercury, right? It's the closest planet to the Sun. You'd lose that bet. The winner is hiding under a thick blanket next door.

cards.headline: The rocky four
cards.body: Mercury, Venus, Earth and Mars are small worlds of rock and metal. You could stand on any of them. You wouldn't enjoy most of them. Take Mercury: about 430 °C in the day, then about −180 °C at night. It's the closest planet to the Sun, and it still can't keep warm.

cards.headline: Venus: a runaway greenhouse
cards.body: Venus wears a thick blanket of carbon dioxide. Sunlight gets in, but the heat can't get back out, so it piles up. The result is a surface over 450 °C, hotter than Mercury despite being farther from the Sun. The air is so heavy that the pressure on the ground is about 90 times Earth's. Mercury gets the sunshine. Venus keeps the heat.

cards.fact: Mars is red because it's rusty.
cards.context: Seriously. Iron oxide, the same stuff as the rust on an old bike, coats Martian dust and rocks, and fine red dust in the air tints the whole planet. That air is thin, too: less than 1% of Earth's air pressure. Venus's air would crush you. Mars's barely shows up.

title: Why We Have Seasons
objective: After this level you can explain that seasons come from Earth's tilt, not its distance from the Sun.
summary: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. Each hemisphere takes turns leaning toward the Sun, which is why seasons are opposite north and south.

cards.headline: Most people get this one wrong: summer isn't when Earth is closest to the Sun.
cards.body: It's the obvious guess: summer is hot because Earth swings closer to the Sun. Nice guess. The calendar disagrees.

cards.fact: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January.
cards.context: That's the middle of winter in the Northern Hemisphere. If distance ran the seasons, New Year's Day would be beach weather in New York. Instead, northern summer arrives when Earth is farther from the Sun. So distance can't be what makes summer. Something else is in charge.

cards.headline: It's the tilt
cards.body: Earth's axis is tilted about 23.5°. When your half of the planet leans toward the Sun, sunlight hits the ground more directly and days last longer, so more energy lands on each patch of ground. That's summer. Lean away, and the same sunlight arrives at a slant and spreads thin, like a flashlight beam tipped across a table. That's winter. Same Sun, different angle.

cards.headline: Opposite seasons
cards.body: Here's the proof it's the lean. The two hemispheres tilt opposite ways, so they take turns. In December, New York shivers while Sydney has summer. In July it flips: summer up north, winter in Australia. Same planet, same trip around the Sun, opposite seasons. Somewhere on Earth, someone is always wearing a scarf.

title: The Moon's Changing Face
objective: After this level you can explain Moon phases and why we only ever see one side of the Moon.
summary: Phases show how much of the Moon's sunlit half faces us, over a ~29.5-day cycle. The Moon is tidally locked, so the same side always faces Earth.

cards.headline: The Moon doesn't change shape. You're just seeing it from a different angle.
cards.body: Tonight a thin crescent, next week a full circle. The Moon seems to grow and shrink, but it's the same Moon the whole time. What changes is how you're looking at it.

cards.headline: Half lit, always
cards.body: The Sun always lights up half of the Moon. As the Moon orbits Earth, we see different amounts of that sunlit half: a thin crescent, a half, the full face, then back again. Nothing is covering the Moon; only our viewing angle changes. Try it with a lamp and a ball held at arm's length, turning slowly, and you'll get phases in your living room.
cards.callout: One full cycle of phases: about 29.5 days

cards.fact: We always see the same side of the Moon.
cards.context: The Moon is tidally locked: it rotates exactly once per orbit, so the same face always points at us. Walk a circle around a chair while always facing it, and you'll have turned all the way around once too. And the 'dark side'? Not dark at all. The far side gets as much sunlight as the near side. We just never get to see it from Earth.

title: Eclipses and a Cosmic Coincidence
objective: After this level you can tell solar from lunar eclipses and explain why the Moon can exactly cover the Sun.
summary: A solar eclipse is the Moon blocking the Sun; a lunar eclipse is Earth's shadow on the Moon. The Sun is ~400× wider and ~400× farther than the Moon.

cards.headline: By pure luck, the Moon is exactly the right size to blot out the Sun.
cards.body: The Sun is enormous and the Moon is small, yet the Moon can cover the Sun completely. It isn't design. It's a coincidence of two numbers.

items.label: Lunar eclipse

Earth's shadow falls on the Moon

cards.fact: The Sun is about 400 times wider than the Moon, and about 400 times farther away.
cards.context: Those two numbers cancel out, so the Sun and Moon look almost exactly the same size in our sky. It's the same trick as hiding a faraway building behind your thumb. That's why, in a total solar eclipse, the Moon can cover the Sun's bright disc and reveal its faint outer glow, the corona. The Sun is 400 times bigger. It's also 400 times farther. Tie.

title: Light-Years: Measuring the Unmeasurable
objective: After this level you can explain what a light-year measures and how far the nearest star is.
summary: A light-year is a distance: about 9.46 trillion km. The nearest star after the Sun, Proxima Centauri, is about 4.2 light-years away.

cards.headline: A light-year sounds like a unit of time. It isn't.
cards.body: It has 'year' right there in the name, so it's a fair guess. But a light-year is a ruler, not a clock.

cards.headline: Distance, measured in light
cards.body: A light-year is how far light travels in one year: about 9.46 trillion kilometers. So it's a distance, the way a mile is. Kilometers are great for a road trip. Out among the stars they pile up into numbers nobody can read, so astronomers switched to a bigger ruler.

cards.headline: Why measure space in light?
cards.body: Light is the fastest thing there is, which makes it a handy measuring tape. It crosses from the Moon to Earth in just over a second. From the Sun, it takes about 8 minutes (Level 1's slightly late Sun). So the Moon is about one light-second away and the Sun about 8 light-minutes. Past the Sun, even light needs years, and the ruler grows to match.

cards.fact: The closest star after the Sun is Proxima Centauri, about 4.2 light-years away.
cards.context: So its light takes about 4.2 years to reach us. Moon: a second. Sun: 8 minutes. Next star: more than four years. And that's the closest one; every other star is even farther. Proxima is our next-door neighbor. The street is just very, very long.

title: The Life of a Star
objective: After this level you can read a star's temperature from its color and outline how the Sun will end.
summary: Stars are born in clouds of gas and dust. Blue stars are hottest, red coolest. The Sun will become a red giant and then a white dwarf; massive stars can go supernova.

cards.headline: Stars have a life story: birth, a long middle age, and a very dramatic ending.
cards.body: Level 2 told you the Sun is middle-aged. So what comes next? Here's the Sun's whole story, plus a trick for reading any star's temperature just by its color.

cards.headline: Color is temperature
cards.body: Look closely and stars have colors, and each color is a thermometer reading. Blue stars are the hottest; red stars are the coolest. That's backwards from your kitchen tap, where red means hot. The Sun sits in the middle: it shines white from space, and our air scatters away some of its blue light, so it looks yellowish from the ground.

cards.headline: Bigger stars, bigger endings
cards.body: Relax: the Sun won't explode. It isn't massive enough. Stars much more massive than the Sun get a far louder exit: a supernova, an explosion that can briefly outshine a whole galaxy. Picture one dying star, for a moment, brighter than every other star in its galaxy put together. The Sun's quiet ending sounds better already.

cards.headline: Our galaxy
cards.body: The Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across. A light-year is a distance, so light leaving one edge would take about 100,000 years to reach the other. In Level 8, Proxima Centauri at 4.2 light-years felt far. Our galaxy is more than 20,000 times wider than that. The suburbs are big.

cards.context: You could line up 25 Milky Ways in that gap. Yet on a dark night you can see Andromeda with the naked eye, as a faint smudge. That smudge is a whole galaxy, and the light reaching your eye took about 2.5 million years to get here.

cards.headline: And then everything else
cards.body: Andromeda is just one galaxy. The observable universe holds billions of galaxies, many with billions of stars each. And the universe itself is about 13.8 billion years old, about three times the Sun's age. So here's the full address: one planet, around one star, in one galaxy among billions.

title: Why the Sky Turns
objective: After this level you can explain that day and night, and the stars rising and setting, come from Earth spinning.
summary: Earth spins once a day from west to east, so the Sun and stars appear to rise in the east and set in the west.

cards.headline: The sky isn't turning. You are.
cards.body: Every sunrise looks like the Sun climbing up to meet you. It isn't going anywhere. Your patch of Earth is rolling toward it, and all night long the stars play the very same trick.

cards.headline: One spin, one day
cards.body: Earth spins on its axis, an imaginary line through the North and South Poles, about once every 24 hours. At any moment, the half facing the Sun has day and the half facing away has night. Nobody switches the Sun off at bedtime. Earth's spin simply carries your side of the planet from the sunny half into the dark one, and back again by breakfast.

cards.headline: Why everything rises in the east
cards.body: Earth spins from west to east, so your eastern horizon turns toward the Sun first. From where you stand, the Sun seems to climb up in the east and sink in the west. The Moon, the planets and the stars do exactly the same, for exactly the same reason. They aren't parading around us. Earth's spin sweeps them all across the sky the same way, like scenery sliding past a train window.

cards.fact: At the equator, Earth's surface moves at about 1,670 km/h.
cards.context: So why don't you feel it? Because you, the ground and the air all move together at a steady speed. Nothing rushes past you, so there's no wind in your hair and no coffee in your lap. The whole planet is one very smooth ride.

title: A Year Around the Sun
objective: After this level you can explain what a year is, why leap years exist, and why the night sky changes with the seasons.
summary: A year is one orbit of about 365.25 days. The quarter-days add up to leap days, and the night sky shifts as we orbit.

cards.headline: A year is just one lap.
cards.body: Every birthday, you've ridden once around the Sun since the last one. The candles on your cake are really a lap counter.

cards.headline: One lap, one year
cards.body: Earth takes about 365.25 days to orbit the Sun once, and that lap is what we call a year. It's no gentle stroll, either. Earth races along its orbit at about 30 km every second. Count to ten and you've traveled about 300 km through space, without ever leaving your chair.

cards.headline: Where the quarter-days go
cards.body: Calendars count 365 days, but each orbit takes about 365.25. That spare quarter of a day looks harmless, yet it piles up: after four years, the calendar is a whole day behind Earth. So about every four years we add February 29 to catch up and keep the calendar in step with the seasons. Leap day is the calendar settling its debts.

cards.headline: A different night sky each season
cards.body: At night, your side of Earth faces away from the Sun, out into space. As Earth moves along its orbit, that night-time view swings toward different parts of space, so each season gets its own constellations. That's why Orion is a winter evening sight in the Northern Hemisphere. The view out of the back window changes as you go around the track.

title: Connect the Dots: Constellations
objective: After this level you can explain what a constellation is and why its stars usually aren’t near each other.
summary: There are 88 official constellations covering the sky. Their stars only line up from our viewpoint.

cards.headline: Orion isn't really a hunter, and his stars aren't even neighbors.
cards.body: A constellation is a picture we see from one spot in space: Earth. So what's actually up there?

cards.headline: From pictures to borders
cards.body: People have long joined up the stars into patterns and named them after figures, animals and objects. Today astronomers go further: the sky is divided into 88 official constellations, each one a region with set boundaries, like countries on a map. Together they cover the whole sky, so every star lands in some constellation, even the ones that aren't part of any picture.

cards.headline: A trick of perspective
cards.body: Stars that look side by side can be very different distances from Earth. Remember light-years from Level 8? One star in a pattern could be a few dozen light-years away, its neighbor hundreds. They only look close together from where we stand, the way a faraway streetlight can seem to sit right next to your neighbor's porch light.

cards.fact: The Big Dipper is not a constellation.
cards.context: It's an asterism: a familiar star pattern that isn't one of the official constellations. The Dipper is part of the constellation Ursa Major, the Great Bear. So if you've ever spotted the saucepan, congratulations: you've also seen part of a bear.

title: The North Star
objective: After this level you can find north with Polaris and explain why some stars never set.
summary: Polaris sits above the North Pole, so it stays put while the sky wheels around it. Its height gives your latitude.

cards.headline: One star barely moves all night. Find it, and you've found north.
cards.body: Watch the sky for a few hours and the stars wheel slowly around. All but one, which sits almost still, as if the whole sky were pinned to it.

cards.headline: The star above the pole
cards.body: That star is Polaris, the North Star, and it lies almost directly above Earth's North Pole. As Earth spins, every other star circles around it while Polaris stays nearly fixed, like the hub of a turning wheel. Face it and you're facing north. One surprise: it isn't the brightest star in the sky. That's Sirius. Polaris is famous for where it sits, not how it shines.

cards.headline: Stars that never set
cards.body: From mid-northern latitudes, stars close to Polaris trace small circles around it that never dip below the horizon. They're called circumpolar stars. While the rest of the sky rises and sets, these never leave: their circles around the pole stay above the horizon all night. And Polaris doubles as a free GPS. Its height above your horizon, in degrees, roughly equals your latitude.

cards.fact: Polaris won't be the North Star forever.
cards.context: Earth's axis slowly wobbles like a spinning top, tracing a circle about every 26,000 years, so over the ages the pole points at different stars. The Southern Hemisphere already knows the feeling: it has no bright pole star at all, so navigators there have used the Southern Cross to find south.

title: The Ecliptic: The Planets’ Highway
objective: After this level you can explain why the Sun, Moon and planets all travel along the same narrow band of sky.
summary: The ecliptic is the Sun’s yearly path. The Moon and planets stay near it because the solar system is flat.

cards.headline: The planets don't roam the whole sky. They stick to one narrow road.
cards.body: The Sun, the Moon and every planet keep to the same slim strip of sky. It's no coincidence. It's a clue to the shape of the solar system.

cards.headline: The Sun's yearly path
cards.body: As Earth orbits, the Sun seems to drift slowly against the background stars, and after a year it's back where it started. The path the Sun appears to follow across the sky over a year is called the ecliptic. The zodiac constellations lie along it, plus a 13th that tradition leaves out: Ophiuchus. Sorry, Ophiuchus.
cards.callout: Ecliptic = the Sun's path over a year

cards.headline: A flat solar system
cards.body: Why does everything use the same road? The planets all orbit the Sun in nearly the same flat plane, and the Moon's orbit lies close to it too. Hold a dinner plate edge-on at eye level and everything on it lines up in a thin line. We're looking at the solar system edge-on from inside, and that line is the ecliptic. So a bright "star" near where the Sun set may well be a planet.

cards.fact: Eclipses can only happen when the Moon is on the ecliptic.
cards.context: The Moon's orbit is tilted about 5° to the ecliptic, so most months the new Moon passes just above or below the Sun's path. Near miss. Only when a new or full Moon lands close to where the two paths cross do we get an eclipse.

title: Wanderers: How Planets Move Across the Sky

summary: Planets drift against the stars as they orbit. When Earth overtakes an outer planet, it seems to go backwards: retrograde motion.

cards.body: It never actually turns around. You're watching from a moving planet, and that changes what you see.

cards.headline: The wanderers
cards.body: Night after night, the stars hold their patterns. Planets don't: they slowly shift position against the background stars as they orbit the Sun, always keeping to the ecliptic road from Level 15. The ancient Greeks noticed these drifting lights, and the word "planet" comes from their word for "wanderer." The stars stay put; the planets go for a stroll.

cards.headline: Overtaking on the inside lane
cards.body: Earth orbits closer to the Sun than Mars does, and it moves faster. Every so often Earth, on its faster inner orbit, catches up with Mars and overtakes it. For a while, Mars appears to slide backwards against the stars, then it carries on forward. You've seen this on the highway: pass a slower car and it seems to drift backwards, though you're both going forward.

cards.fact: Retrograde motion is only apparent.
cards.context: No planet ever reverses direction in its orbit. The backwards loop is a change in our viewpoint, not in the planet's path. Mars has no idea it's doing anything strange.

title: Tides: The Moon’s Pull on the Ocean
objective: After this level you can explain why most coasts get two high tides a day and what spring and neap tides are.
summary: The Moon’s gravity makes two bulges of ocean water. Earth spins through both each day; the Sun makes tides bigger or smaller.

cards.headline: The Moon moves oceans. Twice a day.
cards.body: Every beach you've ever visited is being tugged by the Moon. The odd part is that most coasts get two high tides a day, not one.

cards.headline: Two bulges, not one
cards.body: The Moon's gravity pulls on Earth's oceans and stretches them into two bulges: one facing the Moon and one on the opposite side of Earth. Earth spins through both bulges, so most coastlines get two high tides and two low tides about every 24 hours and 50 minutes. High tide isn't the sea coming to visit. It's your beach passing under a bulge.

cards.headline: The Sun joins in
cards.body: The Sun pulls on the oceans too, just more weakly than the Moon. Around new and full Moon, the Sun, Moon and Earth line up and their pulls combine: extra-high highs and extra-low lows, called spring tides. Around the quarter Moons, the Sun and Moon pull at right angles and the tides are gentler: neap tides. Teamwork makes big tides.

cards.fact: Spring tides have nothing to do with spring.
cards.context: They happen twice a month, all year round, including the middle of winter. They follow the Moon's phases, not the calendar. Blame the name, not the season.

title: Where the Moon Came From
objective: After this level you can describe the giant-impact explanation for the Moon’s origin and the evidence for it.
summary: The Moon most likely formed from debris after a Mars-sized body hit the young Earth about 4.5 billion years ago.

cards.headline: The Moon may be made of pieces of Earth.
cards.body: The leading explanation starts with a crash between the young Earth and a whole Mars-sized world. The Moon is what the crash left behind.

cards.headline: The giant impact
cards.body: About 4.5 billion years ago, a Mars-sized body that scientists call Theia is thought to have slammed into the young Earth. The collision flung debris out around Earth, and that debris gathered to form the Moon. Remember the Sun's age from Level 2, about 4.6 billion years? The Moon showed up early in the story, not long after Earth itself. Earth's worst day, and it got a Moon out of it.

cards.headline: The clues
cards.body: How do you check a crash nobody saw? Start with the Moon rocks Apollo astronauts brought back: they're chemically very similar to rocks from Earth's mantle. The Moon also has only a small iron core compared with Earth. And when scientists run computer simulations of a giant impact, out comes a Moon with an Earth-like makeup and a small iron core. Not proof, but every clue points the same way: back to Earth.

title: Craters and Seas on the Moon
objective: After this level you can explain where lunar craters and the dark “seas” came from and why they last so long.
summary: Craters are impact scars preserved for billions of years; the dark maria are ancient hardened lava.

cards.headline: The "Man in the Moon" is made of ancient lava.
cards.body: Look at a full Moon and you see a face. Look again and you're reading billions of years of history, written in lava and craters.

cards.headline: Scars that never heal
cards.body: The Moon's craters were blasted out by asteroids and comets, and they range from tiny pits to basins hundreds of kilometers across. What's surprising is how long they last. The Moon has almost no atmosphere, no liquid water and no plate tectonics. Nothing wears its craters away, so they survive for billions of years. Every hit the Moon has taken, from the smallest pit to the biggest basin, is still on the record. The Moon never tidies up.
cards.callout: No air, no water, no erasing

cards.headline: Seas without water
cards.body: The dark patches are called maria, Latin for "seas." They're vast plains of ancient lava that cooled and hardened: seas of rock, named for water that was never there. Most maria sit on the near side, the side that always faces Earth. So the "Man in the Moon" isn't just a face. He's a face that's always turned our way.

title: Checkpoint: Reading the Sky
objective: After this level you can explain the everyday motions of the Sun, Moon, stars and planets and the tides they cause.
summary: Spin makes days, orbits make years and seasons, and the Moon’s orbit and gravity drive phases, eclipses and tides.

cards.headline: Chapter 2 finale. Everything in the sky moves for a reason.
cards.body: Sunrise, a wheeling sky, a looping Mars, the tide coming in. It can look like chaos up there. It's mostly a few simple motions, and you now know them.

cards.headline: Spin, orbit, pull
cards.body: Earth's spin gives day and night and sweeps the Sun and stars from east to west. Earth's orbit gives the year and a night sky that changes with the seasons. The Moon, circling us, brings phases, eclipses and, with its gravity, tides. And the planets wander along the ecliptic, with Mars looping back whenever Earth overtakes it. A few motions, one very busy sky.
cards.callout: Spin → day · Orbit → year · Moon → tides

cards.fact: Each star rises about 4 minutes earlier every night.
cards.context: Earth moves a little along its orbit each day, so each night the stars get a small head start. Four minutes is nothing on its own. But over a year those minutes add up to a whole different night sky, one season's constellations at a time.

How the Moon's pull makes two high tides a day, and where the Moon itself most likely came from.

title: The First Sky-Watchers
objective: After this level you can explain how ancient cultures used the sky to keep calendars and navigate.
summary: The sky was humanity’s first calendar and map: monuments, floods, eclipses and ocean voyages were all timed by it.

cards.headline: Long before clocks, the sky was the clock.
cards.body: No watches, no wall calendars, no GPS. So how did people know when to plant, when to celebrate, or which way lay home across the sea? They read the sky, the same patterns you learned in Chapter 2.

cards.headline: Calendars in stone and stars
cards.body: Stonehenge in England is a calendar you can walk around. Its stones line up with the midsummer sunrise and the midwinter sunset, so the Sun itself marks the turning points of the year. In ancient Egypt, the alarm clock was a star. When Sirius made its first dawn appearance each year, Egyptians linked it with the start of the Nile's annual flood. Farmers everywhere check the weather. The Egyptians checked a star.

cards.headline: Records that predicted the sky
cards.body: The Babylonians took another route: they wrote everything down. Their astronomers recorded the positions of the Moon and planets on clay tablets, night after night. Those records became good enough to predict eclipses. They didn't need to know what caused an eclipse. They only needed to know when the last ones happened. Data science, in clay.

cards.fact: Polynesian navigators crossed thousands of kilometers of open Pacific Ocean by reading the sky.
cards.context: They knew the points on the horizon where particular stars rise and set, and steered by them, with ocean swells and wildlife as backup clues. Stars rise in the east because Earth spins (Level 11), so a known star coming up over the water points the way. The whole night sky, used as a compass.

title: Eratosthenes Measures the Earth
objective: After this level you can explain how a shadow and a well let someone estimate Earth’s size over 2,000 years ago.
summary: Comparing the noon Sun in two cities, Eratosthenes estimated Earth’s circumference remarkably well around 240 BCE.

cards.headline: Around 240 BCE, someone measured the whole Earth without leaving Egypt.
cards.body: No satellites, no planes, no trip around the world. Just a well, a pole, a shadow and one very good idea.

cards.headline: Two cities, one Sun
cards.body: Eratosthenes heard a curious thing about Syene: at noon on the summer solstice, the Sun shone straight down a deep well. At the same moment in Alexandria, a vertical pole cast a shadow about 7° from vertical. Same Sun, same moment, two different angles of the noon Sun. If the ground were flat, the two cities would see the same angle. They didn't, so the ground between them had to curve.

cards.headline: From angle to planet
cards.body: That 7° is about one-fiftieth of a full circle. So on a round Earth, the two cities sit one-fiftieth of the way around the globe. Multiply the distance between them by 50 and you get Earth's whole circumference. His answer was remarkably close to the modern value of about 40,000 km. Not bad for a shadow and some multiplication.

cards.fact: Ancient Greek thinkers such as Aristotle already had evidence that Earth is round.
cards.context: Remember lunar eclipses from Level 7? Earth's shadow falls on the Moon, and its edge is always curved. Only a sphere casts a curved shadow every time, from every angle. So Eratosthenes could start from a round Earth and ask the next question: how big?

title: An Earth-Centered Universe
objective: After this level you can describe the geocentric model and why it lasted for more than a thousand years.
summary: Ptolemy’s Earth-centered model used epicycles to match the planets and lasted about 1,400 years.

cards.headline: For 1,400 years, scholars agreed: Earth sits still at the center.
cards.body: Before you laugh, step outside. The ground feels perfectly still, and the whole sky seems to turn around you. The idea fit what people could actually see.

cards.headline: Ptolemy's universe
cards.body: Around 150 CE, Ptolemy described it in a book later known as the Almagest: Earth motionless at the center, with the Sun, Moon, planets and stars all circling it. One snag: planets sometimes seem to go backwards (Level 16's retrograde motion). Ptolemy's fix was to put each planet on a small circle, an epicycle, that itself moved around Earth. Think of a teacup ride: you spin on a platform that is also spinning.

cards.headline: Why it made sense
cards.body: First, you can't feel Earth moving. Second, there was a sharp test. If Earth orbited the Sun, nearby stars should shift slightly over a year, the way a nearby tree shifts against distant hills as you walk past. Nobody could detect that shift, called parallax. No shift, so no motion, it seemed. And the model predicted planet positions well enough to run calendars for centuries. Wrong, but very useful.

title: Copernicus Moves the Sun
objective: After this level you can explain the heliocentric model and why it explained retrograde motion more simply.
summary: In 1543 Copernicus put the Sun at the center, making Earth just another planet and explaining retrograde loops naturally.

cards.headline: In 1543, one book quietly demoted Earth to “just another planet.”
cards.body: Remember Ptolemy's motionless Earth at the center? Copernicus took the center seat away from us and gave it to the Sun.

cards.headline: The Sun in the middle
cards.body: Nicolaus Copernicus published a model with the Sun at the center and Earth as just one of the planets orbiting it. In one move, Earth went from the middle of everything to the third planet out, one of the crowd. A promotion for the Sun, a demotion for us. And the planets' strange backward loops were about to get a much simpler explanation.

cards.headline: Loops without epicycles
cards.body: In the Sun-centered model, retrograde motion is simply Earth overtaking the slower outer planets, like passing a slower car on the highway (Level 16). No extra circles needed to cause it. But Copernicus kept one old habit: he assumed perfectly circular orbits. Real orbits aren't perfect circles, so his model still needed some small extra circles of its own to match observations. Old habits die hard.

cards.fact: Copernicus wasn't the first to put the Sun in the middle.
cards.context: Aristarchus of Samos proposed a Sun-centered arrangement around 1,800 years earlier. It didn't win: the Earth-centered view ruled for about 1,400 years instead. Being right, it turns out, isn't the same as being believed.

title: Galileo’s Telescope
objective: After this level you can describe what Galileo saw that challenged the Earth-centered view.
summary: Galileo’s telescope revealed moons circling Jupiter, a full set of Venus phases, lunar mountains and a starry Milky Way.

cards.headline: In 1610, four tiny moons around Jupiter cracked the Earth-centered universe.
cards.body: Copernicus had an argument. Galileo had something harder to argue with: a better way to look.

cards.headline: Borrowed idea, better instrument
cards.body: Galileo didn't invent the telescope; it first appeared in the Netherlands in 1608. But he built better ones, and in 1609 he pointed them at the sky. The Moon had mountains and craters. The faint band of the Milky Way broke apart into countless stars. The sky had been hiding its details in plain sight, waiting for someone to zoom in.

cards.headline: Moons that don't orbit Earth
cards.body: In 1610 Galileo found four large moons circling Jupiter: Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto. That was bad news for Ptolemy. His model said everything circles Earth, and here were four worlds plainly orbiting Jupiter, not Earth. Earth wasn't the center of every orbit. It wasn't even the only planet with a moon.

cards.fact: Venus has phases, just like the Moon.
cards.context: Galileo watched Venus go through a full set of phases, from crescent to nearly full. Remember Level 6: phases come from seeing different amounts of a sunlit half. Ptolemy's model couldn't produce the full set. A Venus orbiting the Sun could. Second strike for the Earth-centered universe.

title: Kepler’s Ellipses
objective: After this level you can state Kepler’s laws in plain words and explain why planets speed up near the Sun.
summary: Using Tycho Brahe’s data, Kepler found that orbits are ellipses, planets speed up near the Sun, and outer planets take longer.

cards.headline: Planets don’t move in circles. Proving it took the best data of the age.
cards.body: Copernicus kept perfect circles, and they never quite fit. Fixing that took years of careful sky-watching and one very stubborn mathematician.

cards.headline: Ellipses, not circles
cards.body: Johannes Kepler worked from the precise naked-eye observations of Tycho Brahe, the best data of the age. Circles never quite matched them. Ellipses did. His first law: planets orbit the Sun in ellipses, with the Sun at one focus rather than the center. Picture a slightly squashed hoop with the Sun sitting off to one side. Not perfect, just right.

cards.headline: Faster when closer
cards.body: His second law says a line from the Sun to a planet sweeps out equal areas in equal times. In plain terms: a planet moves fastest when it's closest to the Sun and slowest when farthest, like a skateboarder who's quickest at the bottom of the ramp. Earth is closest in early January (Level 5), so that's when it moves fastest. His third law adds that the farther out a planet orbits, the longer its year.
cards.callout: Law 2: faster near the Sun · Law 3: farther = longer year

title: Newton’s Gravity
objective: After this level you can explain how one law of gravity covers falling apples, orbiting moons and planets.
summary: Newton’s universal gravitation (1687) showed one force governs falling objects, the Moon and the planets, explaining Kepler’s laws.

cards.headline: The force that drops an apple also holds the Moon in the sky.
cards.body: Kepler described how the planets move. Newton explained why, and the answer was the same thing that pulls your toast to the kitchen floor.

cards.headline: One law for everything
cards.body: In 1687 Isaac Newton published his law of universal gravitation. Every object pulls on every other. The pull grows with their masses and weakens with the square of the distance: twice as far, a quarter of the pull. You'd feel the difference on the Moon, where surface gravity is only about one-sixth of Earth's, so you would weigh about one-sixth as much. Great news for your high jump.
cards.callout: Twice as far → ¼ the pull

cards.headline: Heaven and Earth, united
cards.body: Here's the big leap. The gravity that makes an apple fall on Earth is the same force that keeps the Moon in orbit and the planets circling the Sun. One force, from your kitchen to the edge of the solar system. It also explained why Kepler's laws work, turning a description into an explanation. It even reaches the beach: the Moon's gravity pulling on the oceans is what raises the tides (Level 17).

title: Measuring the Solar System
objective: After this level you can explain the astronomical unit and how astronomers measured the size of the solar system.
summary: Kepler gave the solar system’s shape; transits of Venus and later radar gave its size: 1 AU ≈ 150 million km.

cards.headline: Knowing the shape of the solar system isn’t the same as knowing its size.
cards.body: Kepler gave astronomers an accurate map of the solar system. It just came without a scale bar.

cards.headline: A map without a scale
cards.body: Kepler's laws gave the relative distances of the planets: Mars orbits about 1.5 times farther from the Sun than Earth does, for example. Handy, but 1.5 times what? The laws gave proportions, not kilometers. It was a street map with the scale bar torn off. Measure one real distance, though, and it sets the scale for all the rest.

cards.headline: Chasing Venus
cards.body: The distance to pick was Earth to Sun, and the tool was Venus. In 1761 and 1769, astronomers spread out around the world to watch Venus cross the face of the Sun. Comparing their observations let them work out the Earth–Sun distance. Today radar and spacecraft pin it down very precisely, no round-the-world expedition required.

cards.fact: 1 astronomical unit (AU) is about 150 million km.
cards.context: That's roughly the average distance between Earth and the Sun, and it's the solar system's standard yardstick. Sunlight crosses it in about 8 minutes (Level 1's slightly late Sun). Mars sits at about 1.5 AU. The map finally has its scale bar.

title: New Planets: Uranus and Neptune
objective: After this level you can explain how Uranus was found by telescope and Neptune was predicted by mathematics.
summary: Herschel spotted Uranus in 1781. Tugs on Uranus’s orbit let Le Verrier predict Neptune, found in 1846 almost exactly where predicted.

cards.headline: One planet was found with a telescope. The next was found with a pencil.
cards.body: This chapter handed astronomers two new tools: the telescope and Newton's gravity. Each one bagged a planet.

cards.headline: A planet hiding as a star
cards.body: In 1781, William Herschel discovered a new planet: Uranus. It was the first planet discovered with a telescope, which means every planet before it had been found without one. The funny part: astronomers had already recorded Uranus several times before 1781. They had just written it down as a star. It was hiding in plain sight, in their own notes.

cards.headline: Found by mathematics
cards.body: Then Uranus misbehaved. It didn't quite follow its predicted path, as if something unseen were tugging on it. Newton's law says every object pulls on every other, so a mystery tug means a mystery puller. Working from those unexplained tugs, Urbain Le Verrier worked out where that unseen planet should be. In 1846 Johann Galle looked there and found Neptune, within about 1° of the prediction. A planet pinned down with math before anyone had knowingly seen it.

title: Checkpoint: How We Know
objective: After this level you can trace how observation and reasoning moved humanity from an Earth-centered sky to modern astronomy.
summary: From Eratosthenes to Bessel, better observations kept testing ideas, until stellar parallax proved that Earth moves.

cards.headline: Chapter 3 finale. The last ancient objection falls.
cards.body: Back in Level 23, the strongest case for a still Earth was simple: the stars never shift. For about 2,000 years, nobody could see them move. Then someone did.

events.label: Eratosthenes measures Earth with the noon Sun
Ptolemy puts a still Earth at the center
Copernicus hands the center to the Sun
Galileo finds moons circling Jupiter
Newton's gravity explains why planets move
Bessel measures stellar parallax

cards.fact: In 1838 Friedrich Bessel finally measured a star shifting as Earth orbits.
cards.context: The star, 61 Cygni, moved by a tiny angle over the year. That shift, parallax, is exactly what the doubters of Level 23 had looked for and never found. It gave the first measured distance to a star, and direct proof that Earth goes around the Sun, just as Copernicus argued. The ground still feels still. It just isn't.

title: More Than Meets the Eye: The Spectrum
objective: After this level you can explain that visible light is one small part of the electromagnetic spectrum.
summary: Radio waves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays are all light, differing only in wavelength.

cards.headline: Your eyes are missing almost everything.
cards.body: Radio waves, X-rays, infrared: all of them are light, and your eyes catch only a thin slice of it. So what is all this light you can't see?

cards.headline: One spectrum, many names
cards.body: Radio waves, microwaves, infrared, visible light, ultraviolet, X-rays and gamma rays sound like a list of unrelated things. They're all the same thing: light. The only difference is wavelength. Radio waves are the longest, gamma rays the shortest, and visible light is a thin sliver in between. Picture a piano keyboard where your eyes can play only a few keys.

cards.headline: Same speed, every kind
cards.body: Here's what doesn't change: speed. Every kind of light, from radio to gamma rays, crosses space at the speed of light. So a light-year (Level 8) is the same distance whether you measure it in radio waves or in starlight. The wavelength rule even runs inside your own little window: red is the longest visible wavelength and violet the shortest. Red and violet are the edges of what you can see.

cards.fact: Human eyes see only wavelengths from about 380 to 700 nanometers.
cards.context: That's your whole window. Anything longer, like infrared, or shorter, like ultraviolet, slips past you unseen. Some animals do better: bees can see ultraviolet light that's invisible to you. On this one point, the bee wins.

title: Starlight’s Fingerprints
objective: After this level you can explain how spectra reveal what stars are made of.
summary: Each element leaves its own lines in a spectrum, so starlight reveals what stars are made of: mostly hydrogen and helium.

cards.headline: We know what stars are made of without ever touching one.
cards.body: You can't visit a star, let alone scoop out a sample. Yet astronomers can read a star's ingredients list. It's written in the starlight.

cards.headline: Lines like barcodes
cards.body: Spread starlight into a spectrum, a rainbow of colors, and you'll find thin dark lines crossing it. Each chemical element absorbs and emits light only at its own set of wavelengths, so each element leaves its own pattern of lines, like a barcode. Spot the pattern and you know which elements are there. It's a checkout scanner for the universe.

cards.headline: Reading a star
cards.body: Astronomers match the lines in a star's spectrum to each element's known pattern, and out comes the ingredients list. The answer, for star after star: mostly hydrogen and helium. That shouldn't surprise you. Remember Level 2? The Sun's core fuses hydrogen into helium. The ingredients list and the recipe match.

cards.fact: Helium was discovered in the Sun before it was found on Earth.
cards.context: In 1868 astronomers spotted a line in the Sun's spectrum that no known element could explain. So the new element was named after the place it turned up: Helios, the Greek word for the Sun. We read the barcode before we ever held the product.

title: How Telescopes Work
objective: After this level you can tell refracting from reflecting telescopes and explain why bigger mirrors see more.
summary: Refractors use lenses, reflectors use mirrors. A bigger aperture gathers more light, so the largest telescopes are reflectors.

cards.headline: A telescope is a light bucket. Bigger bucket, more universe.
cards.body: Catching light is the whole game. The more a telescope catches, the fainter the things it can show you. So how do you build a better bucket?

cards.headline: Lenses or mirrors
cards.body: There are two ways to catch starlight. Refracting telescopes gather it with lenses. Reflecting telescopes gather it with a curved mirror. Isaac Newton built the first practical reflector in 1668, yes, the same Newton who later explained gravity. A lens you look through, or a mirror you look into: every telescope you'll meet picks one.

cards.headline: Why size matters
cards.body: Think of a bucket in the rain: the wider the opening, the more it catches. A wider mirror or lens collects more light, so it can see fainter objects and show finer detail. That's why astronomers keep building bigger. And the giants are all reflectors, because a huge lens sags under its own weight, while a mirror can be supported from behind. Big lenses droop. Big mirrors get a backrest.

cards.fact: The biggest optical telescopes today have mirrors about 10 meters across.
cards.context: Mirrors that size are often built from many smaller segments fitted together, like floor tiles. And the next buckets are already under construction, with mirrors more than 30 meters wide. That's more than three times as wide as today's biggest.

title: Why Put Telescopes in Space?
objective: After this level you can explain what Earth’s atmosphere does to starlight and what Hubble gained by leaving it.
summary: Air makes stars twinkle and blocks much of the spectrum. Above it, Hubble (1990) takes sharp images across more wavelengths.

cards.headline: Twinkling is beautiful. For astronomers, it’s a problem.
cards.body: That gentle shimmer isn't the star. It's Earth's air getting in the way. Lovely for lullabies, terrible for photos.

cards.headline: The trouble with air
cards.body: Stars twinkle because moving pockets of air in Earth's atmosphere bend their light back and forth. It's like looking at a coin at the bottom of a swimming pool while the water ripples. Telescopes get that blur too. Worse, the atmosphere blocks most ultraviolet light and X-rays, and much infrared, before they ever reach the ground. Some of the sky's light simply never arrives.

cards.headline: Hubble, above it all
cards.body: The fix: get above the air. The Hubble Space Telescope launched in 1990 and orbits above the atmosphere, so its images are free of that blurring. Up there, the light the atmosphere blocks is no longer out of reach either. And Hubble is the only space telescope designed to be repaired and upgraded by astronauts in orbit. Now that's a house call.

cards.fact: Hubble helped measure the age of the universe.
cards.context: Its observations helped pin the universe's age at about 13.8 billion years, a number you met back in Level 10. Not bad for a telescope whose big advantage is simply being above the weather.

title: Listening to the Sky: Radio Astronomy
objective: After this level you can explain what radio telescopes detect and why they are so large.
summary: Radio telescopes catch long radio waves that pierce dust and work day or night. Linked dishes act like one giant telescope.

cards.headline: Some telescopes don’t need darkness. They work at noon, through clouds.
cards.body: They're tuned to a kind of light that clouds and daylight can't stop. Meet the telescopes that listen instead of look.

cards.headline: A new window
cards.body: In the early 1930s, Karl Jansky picked up radio waves coming from the Milky Way. Radio astronomy was born. Radio waves pass through cosmic dust and Earth's clouds, and radio telescopes can observe in daylight. A cloudy afternoon? A radio astronomer barely notices. Suddenly the sky could be studied around the clock.

cards.headline: Why the dishes are huge
cards.body: Remember the light bucket from Level 33? Radio waves are very long, so seeing fine detail takes an enormous dish. And when one dish isn't enough, astronomers link many dishes into an array that works together like one much larger telescope. Can't build a bigger bucket? Build a team of buckets.

cards.fact: The Very Large Array in New Mexico links 27 radio dishes.
cards.context: Spread out over up to 36 km, they work together like a single dish of that size. Twenty-seven dishes, one enormous eye on the radio sky. The name isn't modest, but it is accurate.

cards.headline: The newest great telescope sees in heat.
cards.body: Your skin already knows this kind of light. Hold your hand near a warm stove and you're feeling it. Now imagine a telescope built to catch it from across the universe.

cards.headline: Seeing through dust
cards.body: Infrared is the light you feel as heat. Its big trick: it passes through clouds of dust that block visible light, revealing stars forming inside them. Think of a nursery with the curtains drawn, and infrared lets you peek in. There's a second prize. Light from the most distant galaxies has been stretched by the expanding universe into infrared. To see that far away, you need a pair of infrared eyes.

cards.headline: The James Webb Space Telescope
cards.body: Earth's atmosphere blocks much infrared (Level 34), so this infrared telescope works from space. Webb launched on December 25, 2021: quite a Christmas present. Its main mirror is 6.5 meters across, made of 18 gold-coated segments. It orbits the Sun far from Earth, behind a five-layer sunshield about the size of a tennis court that keeps it extremely cold. A telescope that sees heat, parked in the shade.

title: Getting to Orbit
objective: After this level you can explain that an orbit is falling around a planet, and what escape velocity means.
summary: Orbiting means falling while moving sideways so fast you keep missing. The ISS does it at 28,000 km/h; escaping takes 11.2 km/s.

cards.headline: Astronauts aren’t floating. They’re falling, and missing.
cards.body: Gravity hasn't let go of the space station. It's falling the whole time. It just never hits the ground.

cards.headline: Falling around Earth
cards.body: Throw a ball and Earth's gravity curves it down to the ground. Throw it harder and it lands farther away. Throw it fast enough sideways and the ground curves away beneath it as quickly as it falls. That's an orbit: falling forever, and always missing. The International Space Station does this at about 28,000 km/h, circling Earth about every 90 minutes. Around the world in the length of a movie.

cards.headline: Why astronauts float
cards.body: Here's the twist: gravity hasn't switched off up there. Astronauts float because they and their spacecraft are falling together, so nothing presses them against the floor. You've felt a flicker of this on a roller coaster's first big drop, when your stomach lifts off your seat. Astronauts get that feeling all day, every day.

cards.fact: To leave Earth for good, you need about 11.2 km per second.
cards.context: That's escape velocity: about 40,000 km/h. Anything slower stays with Earth, either falling back or circling like the station. Orbiting means falling and missing. Escaping means leaving for good.

title: Mercury: The Scorched Survivor
objective: After this level you can describe Mercury’s extreme temperatures and its lack of atmosphere.
summary: The smallest, innermost planet has almost no air, so it bakes by day and freezes by night, yet keeps ice at its poles.

cards.headline: The planet closest to the Sun has ice on it.
cards.body: No planet sits closer to the Sun than Mercury. It's the last place you'd look for anything frozen. So how does a planet bake and freeze at the same time?

cards.headline: Small, fast and close
cards.body: Mercury is the smallest planet and the closest to the Sun, the little sibling running on the inside lane. It's also the quickest. One lap around the Sun takes just 88 Earth days, the shortest year in the solar system. Live there and you'd get a birthday about every three months. Cake budget: enormous.

cards.headline: No blanket
cards.body: Close to the Sun should just mean hot. But Mercury has almost no atmosphere to hold heat in. By day its surface reaches about 430 °C. Once night falls, there's nothing to keep the warmth, and the ground plunges to about −180 °C. Remember Venus from Level 3? Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, so Venus is even hotter than Mercury, despite being farther from the Sun. Venus keeps the covers on. Mercury kicked them off.

cards.fact: Mercury has water ice in craters near its poles.
cards.context: Here's the answer to the riddle. The floors of some craters near Mercury's poles are always in shadow. Sunlight never reaches the bottom, so the ice survives there. The planet closest to the Sun keeps its ice the way you keep a drink cold at a picnic: out of the sun, in the shade.

title: Venus: Earth’s Evil Twin
objective: After this level you can compare Venus and Earth and describe Venus’s surface and odd rotation.
summary: Venus matches Earth’s size but has 90 times the air pressure, acid clouds, and spins backwards so slowly its day outlasts its year.

cards.headline: On Venus, a day is longer than a year.
cards.body: Venus finishes a whole lap around the Sun before it has turned around once. And that isn't even the strangest thing about the planet people call Earth's twin.

cards.headline: A twin gone wrong
cards.body: On paper, Venus is Earth's twin: it's nearly the same size. Then you read the rest of the file. The air pressure at its surface is about 90 times Earth's, a crushing weight of air pressing on every inch. And the whole planet is wrapped in thick clouds of sulfuric acid. Same size, very different personality. Every family has one.

cards.headline: Backwards and slow
cards.body: Earth spins from west to east, which is why our Sun rises in the east. Venus spins backwards compared with most planets, so there the Sun rises in the west. It's also in no hurry. One rotation takes 243 Earth days, but one trip around the Sun takes only 225. It turns so slowly that it finishes an orbit before it finishes a single spin. That's how a day ends up longer than a year.

cards.fact: The Soviet Venera landers reached Venus's surface.
cards.context: In the 1970s and 1980s, these landers made it all the way down to the ground of Earth's twin. Then they survived only up to about two hours. After the last card, that's no surprise. Two hours on Venus is about the length of a movie, and it was still an impressive run.

title: Earth: The Planet We Know Best
objective: After this level you can explain how Earth’s magnetic field and atmosphere protect life.
summary: A magnetic field from the molten core deflects solar particles; the atmosphere and ozone layer shield us; water covers 71%.

cards.headline: Earth wears invisible armor.
cards.body: The Sun sends out a steady stream of charged particles and harmful ultraviolet light. Life on Earth is fine anyway, because the planet wears layers of protection you mostly can't see.

cards.headline: A magnetic shield
cards.body: The first layer starts deep underground. Molten iron moving in Earth's outer core generates a magnetic field. That field deflects most of the charged particles streaming from the Sun, like an umbrella in sideways rain. A few slip through near the poles, where they reach the upper atmosphere and make the sky glow as auroras. The northern lights are the armor showing where it gets hit.

cards.headline: Air and ozone
cards.body: The second layer is the air itself. Earth's atmosphere is about 78% nitrogen and 21% oxygen, so every breath you take is mostly nitrogen, with about a fifth oxygen. High up, the ozone layer absorbs most of the Sun's harmful ultraviolet light before it reaches the ground. It's sunscreen the planet puts on for you, no sticky hands required.

cards.fact: About 71% of Earth's surface is covered by water.
cards.context: So what is all that armor guarding? A mostly blue planet, and something no other world has shown us. So far, Earth is the only planet known to have life. With 71% of the surface under water, you could argue we named the planet after the wrong part.

title: Mars: A Planet That Lost Its Water
objective: After this level you can describe the evidence that Mars once had liquid water.
summary: Dry riverbeds and ancient lakes show Mars was once wetter. Rovers like Curiosity and Perseverance are reading that history.

cards.headline: Mars has riverbeds. It just doesn’t have rivers anymore.
cards.body: Dried river valleys and old lake beds are carved into Mars. So where did the water go, and how do we know it was ever there?

cards.headline: A thin, dry world
cards.body: Start with the air. Mars's atmosphere is thin and mostly carbon dioxide, with less than 1% of Earth's surface air pressure. Venus has far too much air; Mars has barely any. And the water? Most of what Mars has today is frozen, in its polar ice caps and underground. The rivers are gone. The water is in the freezer.

cards.headline: Clues of a wetter past
cards.body: Mars kept the receipts. Dry river valleys and ancient lake beds show that liquid water once flowed there. Then we sent a robot to check in person. NASA's Curiosity rover, which landed in 2012, found that Gale Crater once held a lake. Picture a crater as dry as a parking lot that used to be a place you could have gone for a swim.

cards.fact: Perseverance landed in 2021 in an ancient lake and river delta.
cards.context: Curiosity showed that Mars once had lakes. NASA's Perseverance rover went straight to one: Jezero Crater, the site of an old lake and river delta. It's collecting rock samples there. If you want to know what an old lake left behind, you go and pick up its stones.

title: The Asteroid Belt
objective: After this level you can describe the asteroid belt and why it never formed a planet.
summary: Between Mars and Jupiter lies a sparse belt of rocky and metallic leftovers that Jupiter’s gravity kept from forming a planet.

cards.headline: The asteroid belt isn’t like the movies. It’s mostly empty.
cards.body: Forget the movie scene where a ship dodges tumbling boulders. Spacecraft have flown straight through the belt without hitting anything. So what is it really, and why is it there?

cards.headline: The planet that never happened
cards.body: The main asteroid belt lies between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. Most asteroids are rock; some are largely metal. It's building material that never got built. Blame the neighbor. Remember from Level 4 that Jupiter is more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined? Its strong gravity stirred up the material there and kept it from ever gathering into a planet. Hard to build a sandcastle while someone keeps kicking it.

cards.headline: Less than a Moon
cards.body: And there isn't much of it. All the asteroids in the main belt together have less mass than Earth's Moon. Spread that thin between Mars and Jupiter and you get mostly empty space. That's why spacecraft have crossed the belt without hitting anything. The movie version needs a lot more asteroids.

cards.fact: The biggest object in the asteroid belt is a dwarf planet.
cards.context: Its name is Ceres, and it's classified as a dwarf planet, in the same club as Pluto. So the belt's biggest resident isn't officially an asteroid at all. In a neighborhood of rubble, it's the one with a title.

title: Jupiter’s Storms and Moons
objective: After this level you can describe the Great Red Spot and Jupiter’s four large moons.
summary: The Great Red Spot is a storm wider than Earth. Jupiter’s four big moons range from volcanic Io to giant Ganymede.

cards.headline: Jupiter has a storm wider than Earth, and it's been going for 150+ years.
cards.body: Last level, Jupiter's gravity bullied the asteroid belt. Up close, the giant is just as dramatic: a storm bigger than our whole planet, and a family of moons that are worlds of their own.

cards.headline: The Great Red Spot
cards.body: Jupiter's Great Red Spot is a giant storm wider than Earth. Lay our whole planet across it, and the storm is still wider. Every storm you've ever sat through blew over in a day or two. Astronomers have been watching this one for more than 150 years, and it's still there. It isn't forever, though: it has been shrinking over the past century. Even Jupiter's weather calms down eventually.

cards.headline: Four worlds of their own
cards.body: Jupiter has around 100 known moons, and more keep turning up. But the four Galileo spotted in 1610 are by far the largest, and each has a personality. Io is the most volcanically active world in the solar system. Ganymede is the largest moon of all, bigger than the planet Mercury: a moon that outsizes a planet. Callisto is one of the most heavily cratered worlds known. And Europa? It gets the next level to itself.

title: Ocean Worlds: Europa and Enceladus
objective: After this level you can explain why icy moons may hide liquid-water oceans.
summary: Europa and Enceladus hide oceans under ice, kept liquid by tidal flexing from their planets: prime places to look for life.

cards.headline: Some of the solar system’s biggest oceans are on moons, under ice.
cards.body: Out past the asteroid belt, far from the Sun, you'd expect every drop of water to be frozen solid. Yet some moons hide liquid oceans under their icy shells. So how do you keep an ocean from freezing out there?

cards.headline: Hidden seas
cards.body: Jupiter's moon Europa, the one we saved from last level, has a salty ocean of liquid water beneath its icy shell. It may hold about twice as much water as all of Earth's oceans put together. Out at Saturn, the moon Enceladus gives its secret away: NASA's Cassini spacecraft saw plumes of water ice spraying from cracks near its south pole. Some oceans hide. This one sneezes.

cards.headline: Kept warm by squeezing
cards.body: The heat comes from gravity. As these moons orbit, their giant planets squeeze and flex them: Jupiter works on Europa, Saturn on Enceladus. All that flexing heats their interiors enough to keep the water liquid. It's a cousin of Level 17's tides, where the Moon's gravity stretches Earth's oceans. Water, energy and the right chemistry are key ingredients for life, which is why NASA launched Europa Clipper in 2024 to study Europa.

title: Titan: A World of Methane Lakes
objective: After this level you can describe Titan’s thick atmosphere and liquid methane lakes.
summary: Saturn’s largest moon has a thick nitrogen atmosphere and lakes of liquid methane; the Huygens probe landed there in 2005.

cards.headline: It rains on Titan. Just not water.
cards.body: Titan has clouds, rain, lakes and seas. It's a weather report that sounds almost like home, right up until you check what's falling from the sky.

cards.headline: A moon with weather
cards.body: Titan is Saturn's largest moon, bigger than the planet Mercury. It's also the only moon with a thick atmosphere, made mostly of nitrogen, just like the air you breathe. Its clouds rain methane, which gathers in lakes and seas of liquid methane and ethane. Why not water? At about −179 °C, Titan is far too cold for liquid water. Pack a raincoat. And a very warm sweater.

cards.headline: Earth's strange cousin
cards.body: Those methane lakes make Titan special. Apart from Earth, it's the only world known to have stable liquid on its surface. Even Europa, with all its water, keeps its ocean hidden under a shell of ice. A place like Titan deserved a visit, and in 2005 it got one: the Huygens probe landed there, the first landing ever on a world in the outer solar system. Of all the far-off places to touch down first, we picked the one with lakes.

title: The Tilted and the Windy: Uranus and Neptune
objective: After this level you can describe Uranus’s sideways tilt and Neptune’s supersonic winds.
summary: Uranus rolls on its side with 42-year polar days; Neptune has the fastest winds known. Methane makes both of them blue.

cards.headline: On Uranus, a single day at the pole can last 42 years.
cards.body: Uranus and Neptune, the two ice giants, are the oddballs of the family. One rolls around the Sun on its side. The other has the fastest winds in the solar system.

cards.headline: A planet on its side
cards.body: Back in Level 5, Earth's lean of about 23.5° was enough to give you summer and winter. Uranus is tilted about 98°, so it essentially rolls around the Sun on its side. That makes for extreme seasons: each pole gets about 42 years of continuous sunlight, followed by 42 years of darkness. Be born at the start of a polar summer, and you'd be middle-aged by sunset.

cards.headline: The windiest planet
cards.body: Neptune has the fastest winds in the solar system, over 2,000 km/h. It's also so far out that one trip around the Sun takes about 165 years, which means it only finished its first full orbit since its discovery in 2011. And visitors are rare: Voyager 2 is the only spacecraft ever to drop by. Windy, remote, and hardly anyone calls.

cards.fact: Methane makes Uranus and Neptune blue.
cards.context: Methane in their atmospheres absorbs red light. Take the red out of sunlight, and what bounces back to your eye looks blue. Two very different oddballs, painted with the same trick.

title: Pluto and the Dwarf Planets
objective: After this level you can explain what a dwarf planet is and why Pluto was reclassified.
summary: The IAU’s 2006 definition requires a planet to clear its orbit. Pluto doesn’t, so it’s one of five dwarf planets.

cards.headline: Pluto didn’t change in 2006. The definition of a planet did.
cards.body: Pluto is the same icy world it always was. What changed in 2006 was the rulebook, and Pluto failed one of the rules.

cards.headline: Three tests for a planet
cards.body: In 2006 the International Astronomical Union wrote the rulebook. A planet must orbit the Sun, be massive enough to pull itself round, and have cleared the neighborhood around its orbit. Pluto passes the first two tests easily. The third one sinks it: Pluto hasn't cleared its orbital neighborhood. A planet owns its block. Pluto still shares its block with the neighbors, so it's a dwarf planet.
cards.callout: Orbit the Sun · Round · Clear its orbit

cards.headline: Five dwarf planets
cards.body: Pluto has company. The IAU recognizes five dwarf planets: Ceres, Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake. You've met Ceres before: in Level 45 it was the largest object in the asteroid belt. It's round and it orbits the Sun, but it shares its orbit with the rest of the belt. Same test, same result. Pluto itself was discovered in 1930 by Clyde Tombaugh, 76 years before anyone wrote the rule it would fail.

cards.fact: Pluto has a heart.
cards.context: In 2015 NASA's New Horizons flew past Pluto and revealed a huge heart-shaped region covered in nitrogen ice. That's nine years after Pluto was told it wasn't a planet, and it answered by showing us its heart. No hard feelings, apparently.

cards.headline: Past Neptune, the solar system keeps going, into the deep freeze.
cards.body: Pluto isn't out there on its own. It's one member of a whole second belt, bigger than the one between Mars and Jupiter and made of ice instead of rock.

cards.headline: A second belt
cards.body: The Kuiper Belt is a doughnut-shaped region of icy bodies beyond the orbit of Neptune. Think of it as the asteroid belt's big cousin who lives in the freezer. The asteroid belt is mostly rock; the Kuiper Belt is mostly ice, and it's about 20 times as wide. Pluto is one of its largest known members, which explains Level 51: Pluto orbits among many other icy bodies of its own zone. It also sends us visitors. Many comets that return every few years are thought to come from here and the scattered disk just beyond.

cards.headline: The farthest flyby
cards.body: After Pluto, New Horizons kept going. In 2019 it flew past Arrokoth, a small Kuiper Belt object and the most distant thing ever explored up close. Arrokoth is thought to be largely unchanged since the planets formed. It's a leftover brick from the building site of the solar system, still sitting in the freezer where it was dropped.

title: Comets: Dirty Snowballs
objective: After this level you can explain what comets are made of and why their tails point away from the Sun.
summary: Comets are icy “dirty snowballs.” Near the Sun they grow a coma and tails that always point away from it.

cards.headline: A comet’s tail can point ahead of it.
cards.body: Picture a comet and you probably see a tail streaming out behind it, like hair in the wind. Sometimes that tail is out in front. The comet doesn't get a vote: the Sun decides which way it points.

cards.headline: Dirty snowballs
cards.body: Comets are chunks of ice, dust and rock, often described as dirty snowballs. Many of the ones that return every few years are thought to come from the Kuiper Belt you met in Level 52. Far from the Sun, a comet is just that: a dirty snowball. As one nears the Sun, its ice turns to gas, forming a glowing cloud called a coma and long tails. A comet only puts on a show when it gets close enough for its ice to start turning to gas.

cards.headline: Tails that point away
cards.body: Sunlight and the solar wind push a comet's tails away from the Sun, always. So a tail isn't exhaust trailing behind the comet. It's more like a windsock, and the Sun is the wind. On the way in, the tail trails behind. On the way back out, it leads the way. Many comets actually have two tails: one of dust and one of charged gas.
cards.callout: Tails point away from the Sun

cards.fact: Halley's Comet returns about every 76 years.
cards.context: It last swung past Earth in 1986 and will be back in 2061. If you missed the last visit, 2061 is your next chance. Set a very long reminder.

title: Shooting Stars and Meteorites
objective: After this level you can tell meteoroids, meteors and meteorites apart and explain meteor showers.
summary: A shooting star is a sand-grain meteoroid burning up. Meteor showers come from comet debris, like the August Perseids.

cards.headline: Most shooting stars are no bigger than a grain of sand.
cards.body: That bright streak you made a wish on was probably a speck about the size of a grain of sand. So how does a speck put on a light show?

cards.headline: Three names, one journey
cards.body: The same bit of space debris gets three names, depending on where it is. Floating in space, a small piece of rock or debris is a meteoroid. When it plunges into Earth's atmosphere and burns up, the streak of light is a meteor: the shooting star you see. If any piece survives to reach the ground, that piece is a meteorite. Handy test: the meteorite is the only one you could ever hold in your hand.

cards.headline: Showers from comets
cards.body: Remember the comets from Level 53? They leave trails of debris behind. When Earth passes through a comet's trail of debris, you get a meteor shower, streak after streak. Most of those meteors come from particles about the size of a grain of sand. A few showers, like the Geminids, come from an asteroid instead. Either way, it's Earth driving through somebody else's dust.

cards.fact: The Perseids peak every August.
cards.context: That's when Earth crosses the debris of Comet Swift–Tuttle. The trail stays put along the comet's path, and Earth reaches it at the same point in its orbit every year. So the Perseids are an annual appointment with a comet's leftovers.

title: The Oort Cloud
objective: After this level you can describe the distant shell of icy bodies thought to surround the solar system.
summary: Far beyond the Kuiper Belt, a vast shell of icy bodies is thought to surround the solar system: the source of long-period comets.

cards.headline: The solar system’s true edge may be a shell of ice no one has ever seen.
cards.body: Nobody has ever seen a single object in it. So why are astronomers fairly sure it's there? Follow the comets.

cards.headline: A giant shell
cards.body: The Oort Cloud is thought to be a giant spherical shell of icy bodies surrounding the whole solar system. Not a doughnut like the Kuiper Belt: a shell, wrapped around everything, like the peel on an orange. It may reach as far as 100,000 astronomical units from the Sun. Neptune orbits at about 30 AU, so the Oort Cloud's outer edge could be more than 3,000 times farther out than the last planet.

cards.headline: Known only from comets
cards.body: No object has ever been directly observed in the Oort Cloud. Astronomers infer it from comets that take thousands of years or more to orbit the Sun: trace their long paths back, and they point to a distant shell all around us. It's like guessing there's a bakery nearby because people keep walking past with fresh bread. The comets that return every few years come from the Kuiper Belt. The ones that take thousands of years come from here.

cards.fact: Voyager 1 will take about 300 years to reach its inner edge.
cards.context: And Voyager 1, launched in 1977, is already the most distant human-made object. Our farthest traveler hasn't even reached the front porch.

title: Inside the Sun
objective: After this level you can name the Sun’s layers and describe how energy travels from its core to its surface.
summary: Energy from the core crosses the radiative and convective zones to the ~5,500 °C photosphere. The corona is over a million °C.

cards.headline: The Sun's outer atmosphere is far hotter than the surface beneath it.
cards.body: Imagine stepping back from a campfire and feeling hotter. That's the Sun. To see how strange it is, go through it layer by layer.

cards.headline: Layer by layer
cards.body: Peel the Sun like an onion, from the inside out. First the core, where fusion happens. Then the radiative zone and the convective zone. Next comes the photosphere, the visible surface: the part you actually see when you look at the Sun (please don't). Then the chromosphere, and finally the outermost layer, the corona.
cards.callout: Core → radiative → convective → photosphere → chromosphere → corona

cards.headline: A slow journey out
cards.body: Energy made in the core can take many thousands of years to work its way out to the surface. Then, once it escapes, it crosses all the way to Earth in about 8 minutes. So the sunshine on your face spent ages stuck in traffic inside the Sun, then took the express lane to you.

cards.fact: The Sun's surface is about 5,500 °C. Its corona tops 1 million °C.
cards.context: Back to the campfire. The core is about 15 million °C, and moving out to the surface it cools, as you'd expect. Then the corona is more than 180 times hotter than the surface below it. Why? Nobody fully knows yet. You can see this puzzle yourself during a total solar eclipse (Level 7), when the Moon covers the Sun's bright disc and reveals the corona.

title: Sunspots and the Solar Cycle
objective: After this level you can explain sunspots and the Sun’s roughly 11-year activity cycle.
summary: Sunspots are cooler, magnetically tangled patches whose numbers rise and fall over an ~11-year solar cycle.

cards.headline: The Sun has spots, and they come and go on a schedule.
cards.body: Dark blotches on the Sun's face grow in number, fade away, then come back, over and over. Why are they dark, and who set the schedule?

cards.headline: Dark, but not cold
cards.body: Sunspots are patches of the Sun's surface where intense magnetic fields make them cooler than their surroundings. Cooler means darker, so they show up as dark blotches. But cool is relative: the surface around them is about 5,500 °C (Level 56). A sunspot only looks dark because it sits next to something brighter, like a candle held up in front of a floodlight.

cards.headline: An 11-year rhythm
cards.body: Sunspots keep a calendar. Their number rises and falls in a solar cycle that lasts about 11 years. At the busy end, the Sun is freckled with spots. Near solar minimum, it can go for days with no visible sunspots at all. Then the count climbs again. Call it the Sun's very slow breathing.

cards.fact: Galileo watched sunspots too.
cards.context: In the early 1600s he was among the first to observe sunspots with a telescope. He saw them move across the Sun's face and used that motion to show that the Sun rotates. The spots were riding along like stickers on a spinning ball.
