title: Solar Storms and Auroras
objective: After this level you can explain how solar wind and eruptions cause auroras and space weather.
summary: The solar wind and eruptions like flares and CMEs drive auroras and space weather that can disrupt satellites and power grids.

cards.headline: The Sun has weather, and it reaches all the way to us.
cards.body: Not rain or snow: a wind made of charged particles, plus the occasional storm that can light up your sky or knock out your power.

cards.headline: Wind and storms
cards.body: The Sun never stops blowing. It constantly sends a stream of charged particles into space: the solar wind. That's the everyday weather. Then come the storms. Solar flares are sudden bursts of radiation. Coronal mass ejections hurl huge clouds of charged particles into space, like the Sun sneezing in our general direction.

cards.headline: When storms arrive
cards.body: Earth carries an umbrella: its magnetic field deflects most of those particles (Level 43). Without it, far more would reach the atmosphere directly. The few that get through near the poles reach the upper atmosphere, and the sky there glows as auroras. Strong storms can also disrupt satellites, radio communications and power grids. The prettiest weather on Earth has a mean streak.

cards.fact: The Carrington Event of 1859 is the strongest solar storm on record.
cards.context: It produced auroras seen far from the poles, well outside their usual home. Now picture a storm like that hitting today's world of satellites, radio and power grids. Strong storms can disrupt all three.

title: How the Solar System Formed
objective: After this level you can outline how the Sun and planets formed from a collapsing cloud of gas and dust.
summary: A collapsing, spinning cloud flattened into a disk: the Sun at its center, rocky planets inside the frost line, giants outside.

cards.headline: Every planet, moon and comet began as part of one cloud.
cards.body: The Sun, Earth, Jupiter, the comets from the last few levels: one family, born from the same cloud. And the planets still move in a way that gives the family secret away.

cards.headline: A spinning cloud collapses
cards.body: About 4.6 billion years ago, a cloud of gas and dust began collapsing under its own gravity. As it shrank, it spun faster and flattened into a disk, like pizza dough spun in the air. The young Sun formed at the center. That's why the planets still orbit in nearly the same plane, and why they all stay close to the ecliptic from Level 15. The solar system still has the shape of that one flat, spinning disk.

cards.headline: The frost line
cards.body: Where a planet formed decided what it became. Close to the young Sun it was too hot for ices to form, so only rock could clump together into the small, rocky planets. Farther out, beyond the frost line, ices could condense too. More ingredients meant more to build with, and the giant planets grew huge. Earth is rocky because it was born on the warm side of the line.

title: Checkpoint: The Sun’s Domain

cards.headline: Chapter 6 finale. Where does the solar system actually end?
cards.body: It depends on what you measure. The Kuiper Belt keeps going past Neptune, the solar wind blows farther still, and the Sun's gravity reaches farthest of all.

cards.headline: The Sun's bubble
cards.body: Remember the solar wind from Level 58? It blows a vast bubble around the Sun and planets called the heliosphere. Its outer edge, the heliopause, is where the solar wind gives way to interstellar space. Voyager 1 crossed it in 2012. By that measure, our most distant spacecraft has left home.

cards.headline: But gravity reaches farther
cards.body: By another measure, it's still in the front yard. The Sun's gravity holds on far beyond the heliosphere, out to the Oort Cloud, the outermost part of the solar system, which may reach 100,000 AU. Voyager 1 won't reach even its inner edge for about 300 years. Asteroid belt, Kuiper Belt, Oort Cloud: the Sun's domain runs much farther than its planets.

title: Parallax: Measuring the Stars
objective: After this level you can explain how parallax measures the distance to nearby stars.
summary: Nearby stars shift slightly as Earth orbits; the smaller the shift, the farther the star. Gaia has measured over a billion.

cards.headline: Blink one eye, then the other. That jump is how we measure the stars.
cards.body: Hold up a finger and blink: it hops against the wall behind it. Now swap your two eyes for two spots on Earth’s orbit, and your finger for a nearby star. How far it hops tells you how far away it is.

cards.headline: Earth is the head that moves
cards.body: Your eyes see your finger from two spots a few centimeters apart. Astronomers use two spots on Earth’s orbit around the Sun. Look at a nearby star, then look again half a year later from the far side of the orbit, and the star seems to shift slightly against the more distant stars behind it. That shift is called parallax. The star didn’t move. You did.

cards.headline: Closer shifts more
cards.body: Try the finger trick with your arm stretched out. The hop shrinks. Stars work the same way: the closer the star, the bigger its parallax shift, so measuring the shift gives you its distance. Even for nearby stars the shift is so tiny that ancient observers never detected it. Astronomers still built a unit on it: a parsec, the distance at which the shift would be one arcsecond, is about 3.26 light-years.

cards.fact: The Gaia spacecraft has measured more than a billion stars.
cards.context: The European Space Agency’s Gaia has mapped the positions and distances of more than a billion stars across our galaxy. It’s the finger trick from this level, done with extreme patience and no fingers.

title: Bright or Close? Luminosity
objective: After this level you can explain the difference between how bright a star looks and how bright it really is.
summary: A star’s apparent brightness depends on its luminosity and its distance, fading with the square of distance.

cards.headline: The brightest star in the sky has a secret: it lives nearby.
cards.body: Sirius outshines every other star in the night sky. But a star can look bright for two very different reasons, and Sirius has help from the easier one.

cards.headline: Two kinds of bright
cards.body: A porch light next door can outshine a stadium floodlight across town. Stars play the same trick on you. How bright a star looks from Earth depends on two things: how much light it actually gives off, called its luminosity, and how far away it is. So a star that looks bright might be truly powerful, or just close.

cards.headline: Fading with distance
cards.body: Distance dims starlight fast. A star’s apparent brightness falls with the square of its distance: move a star twice as far away and it looks only a quarter as bright. Ten times as far? A hundredth. If that rule sounds familiar, it should: gravity in Level 27 weakens with the square of distance too. The universe likes this pattern.

cards.fact: Sirius, the brightest night-time star, is about 8.6 light-years away.
cards.context: Sirius really is more luminous than the Sun, and it’s also relatively close. Power plus proximity: that’s the winning combination. A star with more power but far more distance can easily lose the contest.

title: The H–R Diagram
objective: After this level you can read the basic pattern of the Hertzsprung–Russell diagram.
summary: Plot stars by luminosity and temperature and a pattern appears: the main sequence, with giants above and white dwarfs below.

cards.headline: Put every star on one chart and a hidden pattern jumps out.
cards.body: Plot each star by two numbers, the way you might plot people by height and weight. You’d expect a random scatter. Instead, most stars fall into line.

cards.headline: Luminosity versus temperature
cards.body: The Hertzsprung–Russell diagram, or H–R diagram, plots stars by luminosity and surface temperature. More luminous stars sit higher up. Hotter stars sit farther left, which feels like a map with west on the right. Remember Level 9: blue stars are the hottest, so they land on the left and red ones on the right. Ejnar Hertzsprung and Henry Norris Russell developed the chart independently in the early 1900s. Two people, one great idea.

cards.headline: Where the stars fall
cards.body: Most stars fall along a diagonal band called the main sequence. The Sun sits near its middle, which sounds average, but it isn’t: the most common stars are dim red dwarfs, so the Sun is hotter and brighter than most. Off the band live the oddballs. Red giants sit in the upper right: cool but very luminous. White dwarfs sit in the lower left: hot but dim. The Sun will visit both corners one day, red giant first, white dwarf last.

title: The Main Sequence
objective: After this level you can explain why a star’s mass decides its temperature and lifetime.
summary: Main-sequence stars fuse hydrogen. The most massive burn out in millions of years; red dwarfs can last trillions.

cards.headline: The biggest stars die youngest.
cards.body: You’d think a bigger star would last longer. It’s the opposite, and the reason is speed.

cards.headline: Life on the main sequence
cards.body: Remember the main sequence band from Level 63? A star on it is fusing hydrogen into helium in its core, the same job the Sun is doing right now. Stars spend most of their lives this way, which is why most of them land on that band: it’s where they spend their working years. The Sun gets about 10 billion years there in total.

cards.headline: Mass sets the pace
cards.body: A more massive star shines hotter and brighter, and it burns out sooner. The most massive stars last only a few million years. At the other end, red dwarfs, the smallest and coolest stars, are so thrifty that they can shine for trillions of years. Think sports car versus moped: one is spectacular, the other is still puttering along long after.
cards.callout: More mass → hotter, brighter, shorter life

cards.fact: Our nearest stellar neighbor is a red dwarf.
cards.context: Proxima Centauri, the nearest star to the Sun, is a small, cool, dim red dwarf. Like other red dwarfs, it can shine for trillions of years. The Sun gets about 10 billion. Long after the Sun has retired, Proxima will still be at work.

title: Star Partners: Binary Stars
objective: After this level you can explain binary stars and how they let astronomers weigh stars.
summary: Many stars orbit partners. Watching two stars orbit lets astronomers weigh them with the laws of gravity.

cards.headline: Our Sun is a single star. Many of its neighbors aren’t.
cards.body: Being single is perfectly normal for a star. But the ones in pairs have a gift for astronomers: they let us weigh them.

cards.headline: Stars in pairs
cards.body: Many stars orbit a companion, including about half of Sun-like stars. The Sun is single, and that’s no scandal: most stars are small red dwarfs, and most of those have no companion either. Our nearest neighbor, Alpha Centauri, is a family of three stars, including Proxima Centauri. Even Sirius, the sky’s brightest star, has a small, faint partner: Sirius B, a white dwarf.

cards.headline: Weighing stars
cards.body: You can’t put a star on a bathroom scale. But two stars orbiting each other have to obey gravity, so their dance gives them away. Measure how they orbit each other and Newton’s law of universal gravitation, from Level 27, lets you calculate their masses. Some pairs even pass in front of each other as seen from Earth, so their combined light dims like clockwork. Those are eclipsing binaries. Not bad for something you can never touch.
cards.callout: Watch the orbit → get the masses

title: Stellar Nurseries
objective: After this level you can describe how stars form inside nebulae.
summary: Stars form in cold, dense clouds of gas and dust. The Orion Nebula, 1,300 light-years away, is the nearest big nursery.

cards.headline: Stars are being born right now, and you can see one nursery yourself.
cards.body: No telescope needed, just a dark night and the constellation Orion. But first: how does a cloud turn into a star?

cards.headline: From cloud to star
cards.body: Stars form inside cold, dense clouds of gas and dust. Gravity pulls clumps of the cloud together, and as a clump shrinks, its center gets hotter. Eventually the core is hot enough for fusion to begin, and the clump becomes a star. The dust has a catch: it hides the action. That’s why the infrared light from Level 36 is so handy. It passes through the dust and lets us peek inside.

cards.headline: The nearest nursery
cards.body: The Orion Nebula is the nearest large region of star formation, about 1,300 light-years away. Find Orion’s belt, then the sword hanging from it. On a dark night, part of the sword looks like a fuzzy patch. That fuzz is a nursery. Its light left about 1,300 years ago, so you’re looking at old baby pictures.

cards.fact: Hubble photographed the “Pillars of Creation” in 1995.
cards.context: The picture shows towering columns of gas and dust in the Eagle Nebula, where stars are forming. Each pillar is the recipe from this level in progress: gravity squeezing clumps of a cold cloud into future stars.

title: Red Giants and Planetary Nebulae
objective: After this level you can explain how Sun-like stars swell and shed their outer layers.
summary: When the core runs low on hydrogen, a Sun-like star swells into a red giant, then puffs off its outer layers as a planetary nebula.

cards.headline: Someday the Sun will swallow Mercury and Venus.
cards.body: Level 63 said the Sun will one day move to the red giant corner of the H–R diagram. Here’s what that trip looks like, and the glowing mess it leaves behind.

cards.headline: Swelling up
cards.body: When a Sun-like star’s core runs low on hydrogen, the core contracts and heats up while the outer layers swell enormously. The star becomes a red giant: cool but very luminous, so it moves up and to the right on the H–R diagram. In about 5 billion years the Sun should grow large enough to engulf Mercury and Venus, and possibly Earth. Inner-planet real estate: not a long-term investment.

cards.headline: A glowing farewell
cards.body: Late in life, a Sun-like star sheds its outer layers into space as a glowing shell of gas called a planetary nebula. Despite the name, it has nothing to do with planets: early astronomers thought these glows looked like planets’ disks through small telescopes, and the name stuck. Enjoy them while they last. Each one glows for only tens of thousands of years, a blink in a star’s life. Then only the star’s exposed core remains.

title: White Dwarfs
objective: After this level you can describe white dwarfs and why they slowly cool.
summary: A white dwarf is a dead star’s core: Earth-sized, nearly Sun-massive, so dense a teaspoon weighs tons, and slowly cooling.

cards.headline: A teaspoon of this star would weigh several tons.
cards.body: When the planetary nebula from Level 67 drifts away, something is left behind. It’s small, it’s hot, and it’s astonishingly heavy for its size.

cards.headline: A star-sized core in an Earth-sized ball
cards.body: What’s left is the star’s exposed core: a white dwarf. It’s about the size of Earth, but with a mass comparable to the Sun’s. Picture roughly a star’s worth of matter packed into a ball the size of our planet. The result is absurdly dense: a teaspoonful would weigh several tons on Earth. Your kitchen scale would not survive the experiment.

cards.headline: Slowly fading
cards.body: A white dwarf no longer fuses anything. It shines only with leftover heat, like an oven after it’s switched off, and slowly cools over billions of years. That’s why it sits in the lower left of the H–R diagram: hot, but dim. A famous example is Sirius B, the faint partner of Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky. It’s also the most common ending: most stars in the Milky Way, the Sun included, will finish as white dwarfs.

title: Supernovae and Star Stuff
objective: After this level you can explain how massive stars explode and scatter the elements we are made of.
summary: Stars over ~8 Suns’ mass end in core-collapse supernovae, spreading the elements forged in stars, including those in us.

cards.headline: The iron in your blood was made inside a star.
cards.body: Not a metaphor. To see how it got from there to you, follow a star much more massive than the Sun to its very loud ending.

cards.headline: Going out with a bang
cards.body: Stars more than about eight times as massive as the Sun don’t fade quietly like the white dwarfs of Level 68. Their cores collapse, and the collapse triggers a supernova, an explosion that can briefly outshine an entire galaxy. For a moment, one dying star can be brighter than all its neighbors put together.

cards.headline: Cosmic recycling
cards.body: Nearly all the elements heavier than hydrogen and helium were made by nuclear reactions inside stars and in stellar explosions. Supernovae scatter them into space, where they become part of new stars, planets and people. The calcium in your bones and the iron in your blood were made in stars that lived and died before the Sun formed. You are, quite literally, secondhand star.

cards.fact: In 1987, a supernova was visible to the naked eye.
cards.context: It exploded in the Large Magellanic Cloud, a small galaxy near the Milky Way. No telescope required: a star in another galaxy blew up, and anyone under a dark enough sky could watch.

title: Checkpoint: The Lives of Stars

summary: Mass decides everything: Sun-like stars end as white dwarfs, while the most massive leave neutron stars or black holes.

cards.headline: Chapter 7 finale. One number decides a star’s whole life story.
cards.body: That number is its mass. Everything in this chapter, from nursery to final glow, follows from it.

cards.headline: Two paths
cards.body: A star’s final fate depends mainly on its mass. A Sun-like star takes the gentle road: it swells into a red giant, sheds a planetary nebula and settles down as a white dwarf. A star far more massive than the Sun takes the loud road: it explodes as a supernova and leaves behind something much stranger, a neutron star or a black hole. Same universe, very different retirement plans.

cards.headline: What a supernova leaves behind
cards.body: When a massive star explodes as a supernova, not everything flies away. Its core collapses into a neutron star: a ball only about 20 km across, about the size of a city, yet it can hold more mass than the Sun. That’s more than a whole Sun’s worth of stuff in a space you could bike across in about an hour. The explosion is the loud part. The leftover is the strange part.

cards.headline: Crushed to neutrons
cards.body: How do you fit a sun into a city? Gravity crushes the collapsing core so hard that its matter becomes mostly neutrons, packed tightly together. Remember Level 68’s white dwarf, where a teaspoon weighed several tons? A teaspoon of neutron star would weigh billions of tons on Earth. Your sugar spoon has never worked so hard. And many neutron stars spin many times per second, with magnetic fields far stronger than Earth’s. Hold on to that spin.

title: Pulsars: Cosmic Lighthouses
objective: After this level you can explain what pulsars are and how they were discovered.
summary: Pulsars are spinning neutron stars whose beams sweep past Earth. Jocelyn Bell Burnell discovered the first in 1967.

cards.headline: A signal so regular it was nicknamed “LGM”: little green men.
cards.body: In 1967 a radio telescope picked up a pulse that ticked like a clock. It wasn’t aliens. It was something almost as strange: a star keeping time.

cards.headline: Lighthouses in space
cards.body: Remember Level 71’s spinning neutron stars? A pulsar is one of them, sending out beams of radio waves. The beam doesn’t switch on and off; the star spins. Each time a beam sweeps past Earth, we catch a pulse, exactly like a lighthouse flashing across a dark sea. Some pulsars spin hundreds of times every second. That’s a city-sized star turning like a kitchen blender.

cards.headline: The little green men that weren’t
cards.body: The first pulsar was discovered in 1967 by Jocelyn Bell Burnell, then a graduate student, in signals from a radio telescope. The pulses were so regular that her team half-jokingly nicknamed the source “LGM,” for “little green men.” It wasn’t a message. It was a spinning star. The universe had built a clock so steady it looked handmade.

cards.fact: The Crab Nebula has a pulsar spinning at its heart.
cards.context: The Crab is the wreckage of a supernova that Chinese astronomers recorded in 1054. The explosion scattered the star’s outer layers, and its collapsed core became the pulsar, still spinning at the center. Nearly a thousand years later, the lighthouse is still on.

title: Black Holes
objective: After this level you can explain what a black hole is and how one forms.
summary: A black hole is where gravity is so strong nothing escapes. Stellar ones form when very massive stars collapse.

cards.headline: A place where escape velocity is faster than light.
cards.body: Level 37 said you need about 11.2 km per second to escape Earth. Now picture a place where even light, the fastest thing there is, isn’t fast enough.

cards.headline: Gravity wins
cards.body: A black hole is a region of space where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. In Level 37’s terms, its escape velocity is faster than the speed of light, and nothing can go that fast. That’s why it’s black: no light comes out for you to see. Stellar black holes form when the core of a very massive star collapses at the end of its life. Same kind of ending as a neutron star, with an even stranger leftover.

cards.headline: Not a cosmic vacuum cleaner
cards.body: Black holes have a reputation for slurping up everything nearby. They don’t deserve it. From a safe distance, a black hole’s gravity is the same as that of any object with the same mass. Swap the Sun for a black hole of equal mass and the planets would keep orbiting just as they do now. Your days would get a lot darker, but Earth’s path wouldn’t budge.

title: The Event Horizon
objective: After this level you can explain the event horizon and what the first black hole image showed.
summary: The event horizon is the point of no return. In 2019 an Earth-sized network of radio dishes imaged M87’s black hole.

cards.headline: In 2019, humanity saw a black hole for the first time. Sort of.
cards.body: How do you photograph something that lets no light out? It took a telescope as wide as the planet.

cards.headline: The point of no return
cards.body: A black hole has an edge, but it isn’t a surface. It’s the event horizon: the boundary beyond which nothing, not even light, can escape. Outside it, light and matter can still get away. Cross it, and there is no way back. Think of a one-way door with no handle on the inside.

cards.headline: An Earth-sized telescope
cards.body: Level 35 taught two radio tricks: a bigger dish sees finer detail, and dishes linked into an array work like one much larger telescope. The Event Horizon Telescope pushes both to the limit. It links radio telescopes around the world so they work like one Earth-sized telescope. In 2019 it released the first image of a black hole, the one at the center of the galaxy M87. You can’t build a dish the size of a planet, so astronomers borrowed the planet.

cards.fact: M87’s black hole is about 6.5 billion times the mass of the Sun.
cards.context: That’s no collapsed star. It’s a supermassive black hole, the kind most large galaxies keep at their center. Next to it, Level 73’s stellar black holes are pocket change.

title: The Black Hole at Our Center
objective: After this level you can describe Sagittarius A* and how astronomers found it.
summary: At the Milky Way’s heart lies Sagittarius A*, about 4 million Suns. Stars orbiting it revealed it; the EHT imaged it in 2022.

cards.headline: Our galaxy has a monster at its center, and we watched stars orbit it.
cards.body: Nobody can see it. So how do we know it’s there? We watched the neighbors.

cards.headline: Following the stars
cards.body: About 27,000 light-years away, at the center of the Milky Way, stars race around something nobody can see. Picture a racetrack where you can see the cars but not what they’re circling. Astronomers tracked those orbits, and the laws of orbits and gravity from Kepler and Newton turned them into a mass: about 4 million times the Sun’s. One star, S2, laps it about every 16 years. Its name is Sagittarius A*, and it’s a supermassive black hole.

cards.headline: A prize and a picture
cards.body: Watching those stars paid off. Reinhard Genzel and Andrea Ghez shared half of the 2020 Nobel Prize in Physics for discovering the supermassive object at our galaxy’s center. Then, in 2022, the Event Horizon Telescope from Level 74 released an image of Sagittarius A* itself. First we knew it by the company it keeps. Then we got its portrait.

title: Gravitational Waves
objective: After this level you can explain gravitational waves and how LIGO first detected them.
summary: Einstein predicted ripples in spacetime in 1916. LIGO caught them in 2015 from merging black holes 1.3 billion light-years away.

cards.headline: In 2015, humans felt two black holes collide.
cards.body: Not with our hands. With an instrument so sensitive it caught a ripple in space itself, sent out when two black holes merged.

cards.headline: Ripples in spacetime
cards.body: In 1916, Albert Einstein’s general theory of relativity predicted something wild: gravitational waves, ripples in spacetime itself. Drop a stone in a pond and ripples spread across the water. Here, the pond is space and time. The catch: nobody could detect them. Physicists would wait almost a century to catch one.

cards.headline: The first detection
cards.body: On September 14, 2015, LIGO finally caught one: gravitational waves from two black holes merging about 1.3 billion light-years away. To notice it, LIGO had to measure a change in length far smaller than the width of a proton. The discovery earned the 2017 Nobel Prize in Physics. Einstein’s hundred-year-old prediction had finally checked in.

cards.fact: In 2017, two neutron stars collided, and we caught both the ripples and the light.
cards.context: Remember Level 71’s city-sized stars? Two of them merged, sending out gravitational waves and light, and the collision forged heavy elements such as gold. Some gold, it turns out, is made in a crash between two dead stars.

title: Finding Exoplanets
objective: After this level you can explain the transit and wobble methods for finding planets around other stars.
summary: Since 1995, astronomers have found more than 6,000 exoplanets, mostly from the dips and wobbles they cause in their stars.

cards.headline: How do you find a planet you can’t see? Watch its star.
cards.body: More than 6,000 planets beyond our solar system have been confirmed. Thousands of them were caught by the tiny effects they have on their stars.

cards.headline: Worlds beyond the Sun
cards.body: An exoplanet is simply a planet outside our solar system. Most orbit other stars, though some drift freely with no star at all. The first found around a Sun-like star was 51 Pegasi b, in 1995, by Michel Mayor and Didier Queloz. It earned them half of the 2019 Nobel Prize in Physics. Today more than 6,000 exoplanets are confirmed. Our solar system is one house on a very long street.
cards.callout: 1995: the first around a Sun-like star

cards.headline: Dips and wobbles
cards.body: Two tricks do the finding. The transit method watches for the small, regular dip in a star’s light when a planet passes in front of it: a tiny blink, again on every orbit. The wobble method watches the star move. A planet’s gravity tugs it slightly back and forth, and that motion shows up as shifts in the star’s spectral lines, Level 32’s barcodes. One trick catches the shadow; the other catches the tug.
cards.callout: Transit = dip · Wobble = spectral lines shift

cards.fact: NASA’s Kepler space telescope found thousands of exoplanets by watching for transits.
cards.context: It used the transit method, watching starlight for those small, regular dips as planets crossed in front of their stars. Thousands of tiny blinks added up to thousands of worlds.

title: The Habitable Zone
objective: After this level you can explain the habitable zone and why liquid water matters.
summary: The habitable zone is where a planet could hold liquid water. It sits closer to dim stars; TRAPPIST-1 has planets in its zone.

cards.headline: Not too hot, not too cold. Planets have a Goldilocks zone.
cards.body: Around every star there’s a band where a planet could be just right for liquid water. Where that band sits depends on the star.

cards.headline: Just right for water
cards.body: The habitable zone is the range of distances from a star where a planet’s surface could be the right temperature for liquid water. Where it lies depends on the star. Around dim, cool stars like red dwarfs, the zone sits much closer in; around bright stars, it’s farther out. It’s like a campfire: with a small fire, you pull your chair in close.
cards.callout: Dim star → close zone · Bright star → far zone

cards.headline: Not a guarantee
cards.body: Being in the habitable zone doesn’t guarantee liquid water, let alone life. A planet’s atmosphere matters too. Remember Venus from Level 3? Its thick carbon dioxide atmosphere traps heat, and its surface bakes at over 450 °C. The right address doesn’t help if the air is wrong.

cards.fact: TRAPPIST-1 has seven Earth-sized planets.
cards.context: This red dwarf, about 40 light-years away, is one of the small, cool stars whose habitable zone hugs it closely, and several of its planets sit inside that zone. One dim star, seven Earth-sized worlds, and more than one pulled up close to the campfire.

title: The Search for Life
objective: After this level you can describe how scientists look for signs of life beyond Earth.
summary: Scientists hunt for biosignatures on Mars, in ocean moons and in exoplanet air, and SETI listens for signals. None confirmed yet.

cards.headline: Are we alone? We finally have tools that could answer.
cards.body: Nobody knows yet. But the search has a plan: follow the water nearby, and read the air far away.

cards.headline: Close to home
cards.body: In our own solar system, the search follows the water. On Mars, NASA’s Perseverance rover is collecting rock samples in Jezero Crater, the site of an ancient lake. Farther out, ocean moons like Europa and Enceladus keep liquid water under their ice. Why there? Liquid water, a source of energy and the right chemistry are the key ingredients for life as we know it. Call it life’s recipe card.

cards.headline: Reading alien air
cards.body: Around other stars, scientists read the air instead. They look for biosignatures: gases, such as oxygen and methane together, that living things could produce. The James Webb Space Telescope can analyze starlight passing through some exoplanets’ atmospheres to detect the gases they contain. It’s a sniff test done with light, from light-years away.

cards.fact: No life has yet been confirmed anywhere beyond Earth.
cards.context: Not on Mars, not in the ocean moons, not in any alien air. Meanwhile, SETI projects listen for another kind of clue: radio and other signals a technological civilization could send. For now, Earth is the only place we know of with life.

cards.headline: Listening and looking
cards.body: Each discovery in this chapter came from reading a different signal. Pulsars give away neutron stars with radio beams that sweep past Earth like a lighthouse. Gravitational waves, first caught by LIGO in 2015, revealed two black holes merging. And tiny dips and wobbles in starlight have uncovered thousands of worlds around other stars, some, like TRAPPIST-1’s, in their habitable zones. Dead stars and new worlds, found the same way: by paying very close attention.

title: Kinds of Galaxies
objective: After this level you can tell spiral, elliptical and irregular galaxies apart.
summary: Galaxies come in three main shapes: spirals with arms and new stars, smooth ellipticals of old stars, and shapeless irregulars.

cards.headline: Galaxies come in shapes, and each shape tells a story.
cards.body: Look through a big telescope and galaxies don't all look alike. In the 1920s Edwin Hubble sorted them by shape, and the shape turns out to tell you something: whether a galaxy is still making new stars.

cards.headline: Pinwheels and eggs
cards.body: Hubble's first two drawers hold most of the famous faces. Spiral galaxies are the pinwheels: a flat, rotating disk with spiral arms, where young stars are still forming. Elliptical galaxies are smooth, rounded collections of mostly older stars, with little new star formation. One is a busy nursery. The other is a quiet retirement home.

cards.headline: The drawer marked "other"
cards.body: Then there are the galaxies that refuse to fit. Irregular galaxies have no clear shape at all: no neat arms, no smooth oval. Two of the best known, the Large and Small Magellanic Clouds, are close neighbors that orbit our own Milky Way. Every filing system needs a drawer for the rebels, and the universe has plenty of them.

cards.fact: Our galaxy is a barred spiral.
cards.context: So which drawer is ours? The Milky Way is a spiral with a bar of stars across its center, as you first learned back in Level 1. Picture a pinwheel with a stick through the middle. And because it's a spiral, our galaxy is still in the star-making business.

title: Inside the Milky Way
objective: After this level you can describe the Milky Way’s disk, spiral arms, central bulge and halo.
summary: The Milky Way has a bulge, a disk with arms and a halo. The Sun sits 26,000 light-years out and circles every 230 million years.

cards.headline: The Sun has circled the Milky Way only about 20 times since it formed.
cards.body: Right now the Sun, with Earth in tow, is circling the center of our galaxy. It's a very slow ride. Before timing a lap, here's a map of the track.

cards.headline: The anatomy of a galaxy
cards.body: Picture a fried egg. In the middle sits a thick yolk of stars, the central bulge. Around it spreads a flat disk about 100,000 light-years across, swirled into spiral arms. Wrapped around the whole thing is a faint halo of old stars and globular star clusters. And at the very center of the bulge sits a black hole, Sagittarius A*. Not your usual breakfast.

cards.headline: Our place in it
cards.body: The Sun lives out in the disk, in a minor spiral arm about 26,000 light-years from the center. That's roughly halfway to the edge: the galactic suburbs. From there it orbits the center, taking about 230 million years for one lap, a "galactic year." The Sun is about 4.6 billion years old, so it has made only about 20 laps. In galactic years, our star is about 20.

title: When Galaxies Collide
objective: After this level you can explain galaxy collisions and the future merger of the Milky Way and Andromeda.
summary: Galaxies merge over hundreds of millions of years. Andromeda is heading our way, but stars almost never hit each other.

cards.headline: Andromeda is heading toward the Milky Way.
cards.body: Our biggest neighbor is on the move, and it's coming our way. Should you worry? Short answer: no. Long answer: a galaxy collision is stranger, and gentler, than it sounds.

cards.headline: The forecast
cards.body: Galaxies can collide and merge, pulling each other into new shapes over hundreds of millions of years. Andromeda, about 2.5 million light-years away, is moving toward the Milky Way. For years the forecast was a merger in about 4.5 billion years. Then a 2025 study put the chance of one within the next 10 billion years at only about 50%. The sure thing became a coin flip.
cards.callout: Merger: a coin flip within 10 billion years

cards.headline: Crash without a crash
cards.body: Even if it happens, don't picture a pileup. When galaxies collide, individual stars almost never hit each other, because the space between stars is so vast. The two galaxies pass through each other while their gravity reshapes both. Even a full merger leaves almost every star without a scratch.

cards.fact: You can see our galactic neighbor with your own eyes.
cards.context: From a dark site, Andromeda shows up to the naked eye as a faint smudge. That smudge is the galaxy in this story, about 2.5 million light-years away and heading our way. It's the rare forecast you can check from your backyard.

title: The Local Group
objective: After this level you can describe the small group of galaxies the Milky Way belongs to.
summary: The Milky Way is one of about 100 or more galaxies in the Local Group, dominated by us and Andromeda, about 10 million light-years across.

cards.headline: Our galaxy lives in a neighborhood.
cards.body: The Milky Way isn't alone out there. It has a big neighbor, a couple of small hangers-on, and a crowd of little ones. Time to meet the neighborhood.

cards.headline: Two mansions, lots of cottages
cards.body: The Milky Way belongs to the Local Group, about 100 or more galaxies spread across about 10 million light-years. Most of them are small dwarf galaxies. Two big spirals run the place: the Milky Way and Andromeda. Think of a small town with two mansions and a lot of cottages. We live in one of the mansions.

cards.headline: Our satellites
cards.body: Some of the cottages are practically in our yard. The Large and Small Magellanic Clouds are small galaxies orbiting the Milky Way, the irregulars from Level 81 with no clear shape. From the Southern Hemisphere you can see both with the naked eye, as two faint, cloudy patches of light. Two whole galaxies, no telescope required. Just the right hemisphere.

cards.fact: Andromeda is the Local Group's other giant.
cards.context: It's the other mansion, about 2.5 million light-years away, and from a dark site you can spot it with the naked eye as a faint smudge. Remember Level 83: it's also the neighbor that might, someday, move in.

title: Dark Matter
objective: After this level you can explain the evidence for dark matter from how galaxies spin.
summary: Galaxies spin too fast for their visible matter. Unseen dark matter, about five times ordinary matter, holds them together.

cards.headline: Most of the matter in the universe is invisible.
cards.body: Stars, gas, planets, you: everything you can see is the minority. Astronomers found out because galaxies were breaking the rules.

cards.headline: Galaxies spin too fast
cards.body: Remember Kepler from Level 26: the farther a planet is from the Sun, the longer its orbit takes. You'd expect a galaxy to work the same way. But in the 1970s Vera Rubin measured how fast stars orbit in spiral galaxies, and stars far from the center were moving far too fast for the visible matter to hold them. They should have flown off, like mud from a spinning bike wheel. Something unseen had to be adding gravity.

cards.headline: An older clue
cards.body: Rubin wasn't the first to smell a rat. Back in 1933, Fritz Zwicky noticed that galaxies in the Coma Cluster moved too fast to be held together by their visible mass. Same symptom, bigger patient. Today astronomers estimate there's roughly five times as much dark matter as ordinary matter. The stuff we can see is the small print.

cards.fact: Dark matter doesn't shine, absorb or reflect light.
cards.context: No glow, no shadow, no reflection. We detect it only through its gravity, the way you notice wind by watching the trees bend. What it's actually made of is still unknown. Most of the matter in the universe, and nobody knows what it is.

title: Galaxy Clusters and Gravitational Lenses
objective: After this level you can describe galaxy clusters and how their gravity bends light.
summary: Galaxies gather in clusters of hundreds or thousands. Their gravity bends light, magnifying galaxies behind them.

cards.headline: Some of the universe’s best telescopes are made of gravity.
cards.body: No glass, no mirrors, no launch date. Just an enormous amount of mass, bending light on its way to us.

cards.headline: Cities of galaxies
cards.body: Galaxies aren't sprinkled evenly across space. Many gather into clusters of hundreds or thousands of galaxies, bound together by gravity. If the Local Group from Level 84 is a small town, a cluster is a city. And remember Level 85: there's roughly five times as much dark matter as ordinary matter, so much of the gravity holding a cluster together comes from dark matter.

cards.headline: Bending light
cards.body: Einstein's relativity predicts that mass bends light. Pile up enough mass and you get a lens. A massive galaxy cluster bends and magnifies the light of galaxies far behind it, like a magnifying glass held up to the deep universe. Webb's first deep-field image, released in 2022, used exactly this trick: a cluster in front magnified much more distant galaxies behind it. Free zoom, courtesy of gravity.

cards.fact: Most of a cluster's lens is invisible.
cards.context: With roughly five times as much dark matter as ordinary matter, most of the mass bending that light gives off, absorbs and reflects no light at all. So the lens is mostly something we can't see. Astronomers are peering through an invisible magnifying glass.

title: Quasars and Active Galaxies
objective: After this level you can explain how feeding supermassive black holes can outshine whole galaxies.
summary: Most big galaxies hide a supermassive black hole. When it feeds, its glowing disk can outshine the galaxy: a quasar.

cards.headline: Some of the brightest objects in the universe are powered by black holes.
cards.body: Black holes are famous for trapping light. So how can one sit behind some of the brightest things in the universe? The secret is in how it eats.

cards.headline: Monsters at the center
cards.body: Most large galaxies have a supermassive black hole at their center. When one pulls in large amounts of gas, the gas spirals in, heats up in a swirling disk and glows fiercely, all before it crosses the event horizon. Nothing escapes from inside, so the light comes from the gas, not the black hole. It's the meal that glows, not the diner.

cards.headline: Brighter than a galaxy
cards.body: How bright? A feeding black hole's glowing disk can outshine all the stars of its galaxy combined. The brightest of these are called quasars, and they're among the most distant and luminous objects known. One hot disk of gas beats a whole galaxy of stars. The darkest objects in the universe run some of its brightest lights.

cards.fact: The first quasar was identified in 1963.
cards.context: In 1963 Maarten Schmidt worked out that the object 3C 273 was extremely distant and enormously luminous. To shine that bright from that far away, it had to be one of the most powerful lights in the universe. That's a quasar.

title: Hubble’s Expanding Universe
objective: After this level you can explain how Hubble showed that galaxies are moving apart and the universe is expanding.
summary: Hubble showed Andromeda is another galaxy, then that galaxies recede faster the farther they are: the universe is expanding.

cards.headline: In 1924, the known universe suddenly got much bigger.
cards.body: One astronomer, one fuzzy patch of sky, and our galaxy went from possibly everything to one of many. Five years later, he found something even stranger.

cards.headline: One galaxy among many
cards.body: Fuzzy patches like the Andromeda "nebula" were once debated. Were they clouds inside the Milky Way, or separate galaxies? In 1924 Edwin Hubble settled it: Andromeda is a separate galaxy about 2.5 million light-years away, far beyond our own. So galaxies exist beyond the Milky Way, and ours is just one of them. Humbling, and a lot more to explore.

cards.headline: Everything is moving apart
cards.body: In 1929 Hubble reported that galaxies are moving away from us, and the farther away a galaxy is, the faster it recedes. This is Hubble's law, and it means the universe is expanding. Credit where due: Georges Lemaître had proposed the same idea a few years earlier. The universe wasn't just bigger than anyone thought. It was getting bigger.

cards.headline: No center
cards.body: So is everything fleeing from us? No. The expansion has no center. Space itself is stretching, so every galaxy sees the others moving away. Picture raisins in rising dough: from any raisin, all the others drift apart. Sorry, Milky Way. You're just a raisin.

title: Redshift
objective: After this level you can explain what redshift is and how it reveals the expanding universe.
summary: Expanding space stretches light to longer, redder wavelengths. The farther the galaxy, the bigger its redshift.

cards.headline: Distant galaxies look a little redder than they should.
cards.body: It isn't the color of their stars. Something happens to their light on the long trip here, and that change tells astronomers how far it came.

cards.headline: Stretched light
cards.body: Remember Level 88: space is expanding. As light crosses expanding space, its wavelength gets stretched, like a wave drawn on a rubber band as you pull it. Red has the longest wavelength of visible light, so stretched light shifts toward the red end of the spectrum. Astronomers call this redshift: light stretched to longer, redder wavelengths.

cards.headline: Reading the shift

In a distant galaxy, those familiar lines show up shifted toward the red. And the more distant the galaxy, the bigger the shift. Same barcode, slid toward the red.

cards.context: Because redshift grows with distance, measuring a galaxy's redshift tells astronomers roughly how far away it is. The galaxy never has to give you its address. Its light already did.

title: Checkpoint: A Universe of Galaxies
objective: After this level you can describe the universe’s structure from our galaxy up to the cosmic web.
summary: From the Milky Way to the Local Group, clusters and the cosmic web: a universe of galaxies, all moving apart.

cards.headline: Chapter 9 finale. Zoom out as far as galaxies go.
cards.body: Start at home, with the Sun circling the Milky Way. Then keep zooming: our neighborhood, cities of galaxies, and the biggest pattern in the universe.

cards.headline: A ladder of scale
cards.body: Climb it one rung at a time. The Sun circles the Milky Way once every 230 million years or so. The Milky Way is one of about 100 or more galaxies in the Local Group, our small town. Bigger still are clusters of hundreds or thousands of galaxies, cities held together largely by dark matter. And we're not at the top yet.

cards.headline: The cosmic web
cards.body: At the top of the ladder, galaxies and clusters form a vast web of long filaments and sheets wrapped around huge, nearly empty voids. Picture the foam in a bubble bath: galaxies in the soapy film, emptiness in the bubbles. And the whole web is stretching as the universe expands, which is why distant galaxies look redshifted. The largest pattern in the universe is still stretching.

title: The Big Bang
objective: After this level you can explain what the Big Bang theory says and what it doesn’t.
summary: The universe began about 13.8 billion years ago, hot and dense, and has expanded and cooled ever since. It wasn’t an explosion in space.

cards.headline: Everything you’ve met in this course began hot and dense.
cards.body: Level 88 showed galaxies moving apart. So run the movie backwards. Where does it lead?

cards.headline: Rewind the expansion
cards.body: If galaxies are drifting apart today, they were closer together yesterday. Keep rewinding and everything crowds closer, hotter and denser. The Big Bang theory says the universe began in an extremely hot, dense state about 13.8 billion years ago and has been expanding and cooling ever since. So the universe has a birthday, and everything since has been one very long cool-down.
cards.callout: Hot and dense → expanding and cooling

cards.headline: Not an explosion
cards.body: Forget the fireworks. The Big Bang was not an explosion flinging stuff into empty space. It was the expansion of space itself, happening everywhere at once. No center, no blast site, no seat with the best view. The twist: the name came in 1949 from astronomer Fred Hoyle, who favored a rival theory. The most famous name in cosmology was coined by the other team.

cards.headline: The first ingredients
cards.body: In its first few minutes, the young universe made its starter kit: hydrogen, helium and a trace of lithium. That’s it. Nearly every heavier element, from the carbon in you to the iron in a frying pan, would be made later, inside stars. And what came before the Big Bang, if anything? The theory doesn’t say. It tells the story of the cool-down, not what came before the first page.

title: The Afterglow: Cosmic Microwave Background
objective: After this level you can explain the cosmic microwave background and why it supports the Big Bang.
summary: The Big Bang’s leftover light, released 380,000 years in and stretched into microwaves, still fills the sky. Its discovery backed the theory.

cards.headline: The whole sky glows, faintly, with the Big Bang’s leftover light.
cards.body: Your eyes can’t see it. But point the right antenna at any patch of sky and it’s there, waiting.

cards.headline: When light broke free
cards.body: For roughly its first 380,000 years, the universe was too hot and dense for light to travel far, like headlights in thick fog. Then it cooled enough for atoms to form, and light could finally travel freely. That released light is still here. We call it the cosmic microwave background, or CMB: leftover light from the early universe, filling the whole sky. Every direction you look holds a baby picture of the universe.
cards.callout: Released ~380,000 years after the Big Bang

cards.headline: Stretched to microwaves
cards.body: The CMB started as the glow of hot gas. Then it spent billions of years crossing expanding space, and as space expanded, its light was stretched to longer and longer wavelengths, all the way to microwaves. Today it’s only about 2.7 degrees above absolute zero. Same light, same journey: a fiery glow, stretched until it’s barely warm at all.

cards.fact: It was found by accident in 1965.
cards.context: Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson thought their radio antenna had a fault. It didn’t. They had picked up the CMB. The Big Bang theory had predicted a leftover glow like this, so the discovery became key evidence for the theory. Few suspected equipment faults have ever turned out this well.

title: The First Stars and Galaxies
objective: After this level you can describe how the first stars and galaxies lit up the early universe.
summary: After the dark ages, massive stars of pure hydrogen and helium lit up and seeded space with heavier elements. Webb hunts their galaxies.

cards.headline: After its first light, the universe went dark for a long time.
cards.body: When the CMB broke free, there were no stars yet to shine. So who turned the lights on?

cards.headline: The cosmic dark ages
cards.body: Picture a universe with no stars at all: just cooling gas, mostly hydrogen and helium, drifting in the dark. Astronomers call this long stretch the cosmic dark ages. Gravity was busy, though, pulling the gas into collapsing clumps. Within a few hundred million years after the Big Bang, the first stars lit up. The longest blackout in history, ended by gravity.

cards.headline: Giants of two elements
cards.body: The first stars had a short ingredient list: only hydrogen and helium, since that’s nearly all the Big Bang had made. They’re thought to have been very massive and short-lived, the rock stars of the early universe. When they died, they made the first heavier elements and scattered them into space, seeding the gas that later stars and planets formed from. Live fast, die young, leave behind the makings of planets.

cards.headline: Finding the first galaxies
cards.body: How do you photograph the dawn? Light from these early galaxies has crossed so much expanding space that it has been stretched into infrared. So to find them, you hunt in infrared. Webb has already seen galaxies as they were only a few hundred million years after the Big Bang. Those are baby pictures of the universe, taken in a color your eyes can’t see.

title: Dark Energy
objective: After this level you can explain the discovery that the universe’s expansion is speeding up.
summary: In 1998, distant supernovae showed that the expansion is speeding up. Its unknown cause, dark energy, is about 68% of the universe.

cards.headline: The universe’s expansion is speeding up, and no one knows why.
cards.body: Everyone expected the opposite. Then, in 1998, the universe turned out to have its foot on the gas.

cards.headline: Expecting a slowdown
cards.body: Toss a ball upward and gravity slows it down. Gravity pulls everything together, so astronomers expected the expansion of the universe to be slowing the same way. In 1998 two teams checked, using distant supernovae. The supernovae were fainter than a slowing universe allowed. The expansion is speeding up. The ball wasn’t slowing down. It was taking off.

cards.headline: Dark energy
cards.body: Whatever is pressing the accelerator has a name, dark energy, and that’s about all we have: nobody knows what it is. Don’t mix it up with dark matter, which adds gravity. Dark energy speeds up the expansion. Yet dark energy makes up roughly 68% of the universe’s energy content, and dark matter about 27%. Everything made of ordinary atoms, every star, planet and person, is only about 5%. We’re the sprinkles on a very mysterious cake.

cards.fact: The discovery won the 2011 Nobel Prize in Physics.
cards.context: Saul Perlmutter, Brian Schmidt and Adam Riess shared it for discovering the accelerating expansion. Not bad for finding the exact opposite of what everyone expected.

title: How Big Is the Observable Universe?
objective: After this level you can explain why the observable universe is larger than 13.8 billion light-years across.
summary: Looking far away means looking back in time. Space kept expanding while light traveled, so the observable universe is ~93 billion light-years wide.

cards.headline: How can we see farther than light has had time to travel?
cards.body: The universe is about 13.8 billion years old, yet the part we can see is far wider than 13.8 billion light-years. And no, light didn’t cheat.

cards.headline: Looking back in time
cards.body: Level 8 said a light-year is a distance. Light takes time to cover it, so looking far away means looking into the past. We see the Andromeda galaxy as it was about 2.5 million years ago, not as it is today. The most distant light we can see set out about 13.8 billion years ago. Every telescope is a time machine that only goes backward.

cards.headline: Space kept stretching
cards.body: Here’s the trick. While that ancient light was on its way to us, space kept expanding. The regions that sent it are now much farther away than 13.8 billion light-years. It’s like getting a postcard from a friend who has moved far away since mailing it. That’s why the observable universe is about 93 billion light-years across.

cards.headline: A horizon, not an edge
cards.body: So is that the end of everything? No. The observable universe is only the part we can see, limited by how far light has traveled since the Big Bang. It’s a horizon, like the line where the sea meets the sky: the ocean doesn’t stop there, your view does. How big the whole universe is, and whether it goes on forever, nobody knows.

cards.headline: New windows
cards.body: Some discoveries needed brand-new kinds of clues. Stars at galaxies’ edges orbit too fast for the visible matter to hold them, which gave away dark matter, something no one has ever seen. Astronomy learned to feel the universe shake.

cards.headline: Old tricks still work

events.label: Earth’s axis wobbles through a full circle, so Polaris won’t stay the pole star
A slowly brightening Sun makes Earth too hot for oceans
The Milky Way and Andromeda may merge; a 2025 study put it at about a coin flip
The Sun swells into a red giant, later becoming a white dwarf

cards.headline: The universe’s fate
cards.body: Now zoom all the way out. Level 94 showed dark energy speeding up the expansion. If it keeps doing so, galaxies beyond our local neighborhood will eventually drift out of view. Picture a party where the guests slowly back out the door until only your closest neighbors are left. The Sun’s own story ends quietly: a white dwarf that no longer fuses anything, shining with leftover heat and slowly cooling. No grand finale, just a very long fade.

title: Integration: The Big Open Questions
objective: After this level you can describe the major unanswered questions in astronomy and why they matter.
summary: About 95% of the universe is dark and unexplained. The Hubble tension, what came before the Big Bang and life elsewhere are all open.

cards.headline: The best part of astronomy: it isn’t finished.
cards.body: You’ve reached the frontier. Here are some of the biggest questions still waiting for someone to answer them. Maybe you.

cards.headline: The dark 95%
cards.body: Start with a humbling one. Dark matter and dark energy together make up about 95% of the universe, and nobody yet knows what either one is. Ordinary matter, everything we can see, every star, planet and person, is only about 5%. After 99 levels, the honest summary: we’ve mapped the sprinkles. The cake is still a mystery.

cards.headline: Unsolved puzzles
cards.body: Not every mystery is dark. Measure how fast the universe expands today in different ways and the answers disagree slightly, a puzzle called the Hubble tension. The Sun’s corona is far hotter than the surface below it, like air above a campfire being hotter than the flames, and nobody fully knows why. And what, if anything, came before the Big Bang? The theory doesn’t say.

cards.fact: Is anyone out there?
cards.context: No life has yet been confirmed anywhere beyond Earth. But the search now has real tools: Webb can analyze starlight passing through some exoplanets’ atmospheres, looking for gases that living things could produce. For now, Earth is the only place we know of with a pulse.

options.label: A strain on Hubble from Earth’s gravity
options.rationale: It isn’t about the telescope itself.

options.label: Expansion measurements that disagree slightly

options.rationale: Galaxies aren’t being torn apart.

questions.prompt: About how much of the universe is made of things we don’t yet understand?

options.label: About 5%

options.label: About 95%

Scientists agree life is impossible elsewhere

cards.headline: The Astronomy Mastery Challenge.
cards.body: Questions from across the whole tree, from your cosmic address to the edge of the observable universe. Level 1 wrote your address on a postcard; now see how far it reaches. Take your time: every question can be corrected.

cards.headline: Astronomy: mastered
learned: How the universe grew from a hot, dense start into stars, galaxies and the atoms in your body.
Why the Big Bang was space itself expanding, not an explosion, and how its leftover glow backs it up.
Why the part of the universe we can see is wider than light could cross in the universe's lifetime.
What astronomers still can't explain, from dark energy to what came before the Big Bang.

questions.prompt: A friend calls the Big Dipper one of the official constellations. What’s the best correction?

options.label: It’s an asterism, part of Ursa Major
It’s a galaxy, not a star pattern
options.rationale: It’s a pattern of stars.

options.label: It’s one part of Orion
options.rationale: It belongs to Ursa Major.

options.label: It’s a southern-sky pattern
options.rationale: It’s a northern-sky pattern.

questions.explanation: The Big Dipper is an asterism, a familiar pattern within the official constellation Ursa Major.

questions.prompt: Earth is closest to the Sun in early January. Why is January winter in the Northern Hemisphere?

options.label: The Sun gives off less light in January
options.rationale: The Sun’s output barely changes.

options.label: The north is tilted away from the Sun then
The Moon blocks more sunlight in winter
options.rationale: The Moon doesn’t cause seasons.

options.label: Earth is farthest from the Sun then
options.rationale: It’s actually closest in January.

questions.explanation: Seasons come from the tilt, not distance: in January the Northern Hemisphere leans away and gets less direct sunlight.

questions.prompt: Proxima Centauri is about 4.2 light-years away. How old is the light you see from it?

options.label: About 8 minutes old
options.rationale: That’s sunlight.

options.label: Brand new: light arrives instantly
options.rationale: Light takes time to travel.

options.label: About 4.2 years old
About 4.2 million years old
options.rationale: A light-year is the distance light covers in one year.

questions.explanation: A light-year is how far light travels in a year, so light from 4.2 light-years away is about 4.2 years old.

questions.prompt: Why was Bessel’s 1838 measurement of a star’s parallax such a milestone?

options.label: It proved stars are made of hydrogen
options.rationale: Spectra revealed composition.

options.label: It showed the Sun orbits the Earth
options.rationale: It showed the opposite.

options.label: It was the first photo of a star
options.rationale: It was a measurement of a shift.

options.label: It directly showed Earth moves around the Sun

questions.explanation: Parallax is a direct observation of Earth’s motion, and it gave the first measured distance to a star.

questions.prompt: How was helium discovered before anyone found it on Earth?

options.label: A space probe collected a sample
options.rationale: No probe existed in 1868.

options.label: From an unexplained line in the Sun’s spectrum
From the Sun’s yellow color alone
options.rationale: Color alone can’t identify an element.

options.label: From meteorites that fell to Earth
options.rationale: It wasn’t found that way.

questions.explanation: In 1868 an unexplained line in the Sun’s spectrum revealed an element no one had seen: helium.

questions.prompt: Astronomers on the space station float. Which explanation is correct?

options.label: There is no gravity in orbit
options.rationale: Gravity is still strong there.

options.label: The station is beyond Earth’s gravity
options.rationale: It orbits well within it.

options.label: They and the station are falling together
Air pressure inside holds them up
options.rationale: Air pressure doesn’t cause floating.

questions.explanation: An orbit is a constant fall around Earth. Astronauts float because they fall together with their spacecraft.

questions.prompt: A star far more massive than the Sun forms. Compared with the Sun, what should you expect?

options.label: It lives longer, since it has more fuel
options.rationale: Massive stars burn through fuel much faster.

options.label: It ends as a white dwarf, like the Sun
options.rationale: The most massive stars end differently.

options.label: It stays on the main sequence forever
options.rationale: Every star leaves it eventually.

options.label: It burns out sooner and may explode

questions.explanation: More massive stars are hotter, brighter and shorter-lived, and the most massive end in supernovae.

questions.prompt: A planet is found in its star’s habitable zone. What does that tell you?

options.label: Liquid water could exist on its surface
It definitely has life
options.rationale: The habitable zone doesn’t guarantee life.

options.label: It must be the same size as Earth
options.rationale: Size isn’t part of the definition.

options.label: It orbits a star just like the Sun
options.rationale: Habitable zones exist around many kinds of stars.

questions.explanation: The habitable zone is where a planet’s surface could be the right temperature for liquid water, which is a start, not a guarantee.

questions.prompt: Which list puts these discoveries in the order they happened?

options.label: Galaxy redshifts → Jupiter’s moons → the CMB
options.rationale: Galileo came first, in 1610.

options.label: Jupiter’s moons → galaxy redshifts → the CMB
The CMB → Jupiter’s moons → galaxy redshifts
options.rationale: The CMB was found last, in 1965.

options.label: Jupiter’s moons → the CMB → galaxy redshifts
options.rationale: Hubble’s law came in 1929, before the CMB.

questions.explanation: Galileo saw Jupiter’s moons in 1610, Hubble linked redshift and distance in 1929, and the CMB was found in 1965.

questions.prompt: Which is the best summary of where Earth’s iron came from?

options.label: It formed with hydrogen in the Big Bang
options.rationale: The Big Bang made only the lightest elements.

options.label: Earth’s core fused it from hydrogen
options.rationale: Planets don’t fuse elements.

options.label: Meteors create it when they burn up
options.rationale: Meteors don’t create elements.

options.label: Forged in stars, scattered when they died

questions.explanation: Iron was forged inside stars and scattered by their deaths; the solar system formed from that enriched gas.
